 Prologue by Henry Kaufman The word ‘classic' can seem a bit stodgy. Now in this eighth edition,  Manias, Panics, and Crashes  became a classic many years ago, although it is difficult to say exactly when. Indeed, the first edition, written by MIT’s esteemed economic historian Charles Kindleberger, immediately attracted notice and praise. But it is because this book has continued to evolve along with its topic rather than solidifying in its original form that  MPC  still deserves our attention and praise. In retrospect, the Wall Street of 1978—the year the first edition was published—now seems foreign, almost quaint. In the United States, the decade had opened with the spectacular collapse of the Pennsylvania Central Railroad, thanks to its overdependence on commercial paper. Hard to imagine now, the Dow Jones Industrial Average didn’t top the 1,000-point milestone for the first time until 1972. Two years later, Franklin National Bank—a heavy borrower in Eurodollar interbank markets—also went belly up. As the decade wrapped up, another financial crisis roiled markets, this one caused by the Hunt brothers’ efforts to corner the silver market, their positions funded heavily by Wall Street. How many of these events are familiar to today’s investors? More than any other free market institution, Wall Street underscores Joseph Schumpeter’s observation that ‘creative destruction' dooms those who stand still in a capitalist economy. Financial markets have become the epicenters of that reality. The same can be said of those—including the authors of this new edition—who aspire to chronicle the history of extreme financial gyrations.  Manias, Panics, and Crashes  remains a classic, not because it is frozen in time but because—through its various editions and through the contributions of the two co-authors who joined Kindleberger’s original enterprise—it has remained a living document. Some consider me somewhat of a Wall Street ‘classic.' Longevity certainly has played a role: I’ve been a Wall Streeter for seven decades, starting with stints at a commercial bank and at the New York Federal Reserve, then for twenty-six years at Salomon Brothers. The Salomon research departments I oversaw pioneered powerful new methods in financial and business analysis and forecasting—especially regarding interest rates. It was a heady era, one filled with an ample share of booms, bubbles, and busts, as documented in the pages that follow. Along with the US crises noted above, we lived through the collapse of Drysdale Government Securities, Inc. and Penn Square Bank; witnessed the massive bailouts of Mexico and Continental Illinois Bank; and endured the Savings and Loan Crisis. I wasn’t just a passive observer; sometimes my macroeconomic or interest rate predictions moved markets. When after many years of bearish forecasts (some called me ‘Dr. Doom') I released a memo August 17, 1982 predicting the secular reversal of long-term interest rates, markets reacted with the largest one-day bull market since World War II. Living through and somewhat shaping those many years on Wall Street not surprisingly instilled some lessons in me about financial crises. As this book amply demonstrates, excessive use of credit is a common denominator in most crises. Indeed, prior to each crisis, investors typically come to depend heavily on leverage. Excessive credit expansion furthermore is commonly driven by a sense of market enthusiasm, at times even euphoria, or the widespread belief that the old rules no longer apply. Sometimes ‘glamour industries' that drive up stock and bond markets prove to be real; but too often (as with the so-called dot.com bubble) they do not. And not infrequently—as during the classic tale of Wall Street in the 1920s—justified enthusiasm morphs into reckless speculation. One of the great strengths of this book is its melding of history and theory, as in its discussion of the work of economist Hyman Minsky, whose penetrating insights into the dynamics of bubbles and crashes were not fully appreciated during his lifetime. Less well recognized has been the grim fact that the aggressive expansion or over-expansion of credit typically is accompanied by a discernable decline in credit quality. Consider the sharp decline in the number of Fortune 500 companies with AAA credit ratings during the last several decades. Meanwhile, heavy consolidation within the financial sector, including the rise of ‘too-big-to-fail' financial conglomerates, also has worked to undermine the competitiveness and stability of financial markets. As this book generously chronicles and as I learned and often wrote about, US and non-US governments alike have at best posted a mixed record of anticipating, preventing, or correcting financial crises. Even in the modern period, when crises sometimes inspired regulatory reforms, the overall trend has been toward market liberalization and greater risk-taking. It is the great challenge of our financial markets to balance their entrepreneurial drive for profit with their fiduciary role as custodians of our financial assets. Because that challenge is so great—and too often ends in calamity—the story told in thes pages is far from over. In the meantime, we can be thankful this edition of  MPC  brings both history and theory up-to-date in what remains the best single volume on the topic between covers. Preface to the Eighth Edition Charles P. Kindleberger, the second author, has died before the publication of this book. I first met Charles Kindleberger (‘call me Charlie’) in his fall 1976 European  economic history course at MIT . The course eventually became his 1984 book,  A Financial History of Western Europe . In its acknowledgments, he thanked me among many ‘in my MIT classes, some students attending from Harvard.’ In those days, in economics, Harvard was running a trade deficit with MIT, to which I contributed three times, twice with Charlie and once with  Rudi Dornbusch . In 1976, Charlie gave me draft chapters from  Manias, Panics and Crashes . I learned that the 1970s enthusiasm for lending to developing countries had many precedents. Charlie ascribed the 1970s lending boom not to the common explanation of the first oil shock, which flooded banks in London with so-called petro-dollars, but to easy US monetary policy early in the decade and the resultant failure of international monetary coordination: Our problem started with the attempt of the United States in 1971–72 to achieve low interest rates, when Germany was striving to restrict inflation through tight money policies. Money poured out of the United States into the Euro-currency market, and out of the Euro-currency market into Germany and other countries. The Euro-currency market swelled up like a frog in the mating season, and started lending to developing countries in ways reminiscent of the 1820s, 1860s, 1880s, 1910-1913, and the 1920s. 
 1 
 
 
 Sadly, the frog metaphor did not make it into  Manias, Panics and Crashes. 
 Later, I took Charlie’s undergraduate international economics class, using the 5th edition (1973) of his textbook by the same title. This textbook was unusually rich in history and institutions compared to the narrower competing texts. My work over the years probably drew more on this class than any other. At the end of his undergraduate class, he recalled that I had taken his graduate history class and quipped that he expected to see me next semester in his kindergarten class. 
 Paul Krugman  reports that Charlie’s international macro class was ‘full of wisdom’ but left him uninspired—‘who feels wise in his 20s?’. 
 2 
  The history class inspired me to follow in Charlie’s pre-MIT footsteps by working first at the New York Fed and then at  the Bank for International Settlements  (BIS). His erudition, and the way his writing could carry it lightly, were not so easy to follow. What was Charlie’s contribution to  Manias, Panics and Crashes ? One answer is that he applied Hyman Minsky’s model to history, which led him to the prescient forecast that the mania of lending to developing countries would once again see panic and crash. Another answer is Charlie’s argument for the international lender of last resort. Charlie did not just apply Minsky to experience; he memorably formulated a key social psychological insight: ‘There is nothing so disturbing to one’s well-being and judgment as to see a friend get rich.’ On the relationship with Minsky,  Brad de Long  and  Barry Eichengreen  wrote in their forward to the fortieth-anniversary edition of Charlie’s  The World in Depression 
 
 3 
 : Kindleberger amply acknowledged his intellectual debt to Minsky. But we are not alone if we suggest that Kindleberger’s admirably clear presentation of the framework, and the success with which he documented its power by applying it to historical experience, rendered it more impactful in the academy and generally. 
 My experience bears out this judgment. I first saw Minsky at a Federal Reserve Bank of New York colloquium in the early 1990s. He presented his framework with gusto but without applying it to the recent mania for corporate leveraged buyouts or for commercial real estate that drove big US banks to the brink of failure. Colleagues  Judy Ruud  and  Frank Iacono  joined me in applying Minsky’s model to the corporate leveraging mania of the 1980s in  Dodging Bullets: Changing Corporate Capital Structures in the 1980s . In retrospect, what is striking is how little recent material Charlie had to work with. But what he had to work with, he got right. The first rip-roaring financial crisis of global significance after the Second World War came with the developing country debt crisis that hit in August 1982 as Mexico ran out of dollars to service its debt. Charlie had warned over five years before about the accumulation of debt by countries borrowing eurodollars. 
 4 
 
 This ran against conventional wisdom. The tendency at the Federal Reserve and US Treasury was to see the ‘recycling’ of payments surpluses of oil countries as supporting global demand. In a celebrated 1981  Brookings Paper ,  Jeff Sachs  focused on flows and argued that ‘If my analysis is correct, much of the growth in LDC [less developed country] debt reflects increased investment and should not pose a problem of repayment… This is particularly true for  Brazil  and Mexico…’ 
 5 
  In the official sector, few other than  Alexandre Lamfalussy  at the BIS and  Henry Wallich  at the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve shared Charlie’s apprehensions. On the policy front, Charlie’s contribution was to argue for an international lender of last resort. His stint at the BIS in 1939-40 and his following of central bank cooperation there in the 1960s equipped him to recognize central  bank  swaps as the closest approximation to the international lender of last resort. At the time, and for most of the rest of the twentieth century, economists and officials looked to the International Monetary Fund as the closest approximation. Charlie saw from the first days of the swap lines their potential to be extended in an unlimited fashion, anticipating practice in October 2008. With the fifth through seventh editions,  Manias, Panics and Crashes  has another author, Bob Aliber. I first met him in 1991 when he invited me and my co-author  Steve Zimmer  to present our work comparing the cost of capital across countries to his class in international finance at the Graduate Business School at the  University of Chicago . He was kind enough to introduce us as having written an article that he wished he had written. Steve and I had described differences in the cost of capital that Bob had already used to explain why some countries are on balance homes for multinationals (eg. Switzerland) and why others are hosts. 
 6 
  At the time, the competitive challenge of Japanese banks had hinged on their very low cost of equity during the bubble years. Bob nominated me to teach two courses, International Financial Policy and The Multinational Firm, for two terms at the Chicago Business School in 1992. Commuting weekly from New York proved a real treat for me if not the students. Using Bob’s notes to teach these courses amounted to a challenging way of taking his classes. Our dialog since has spanned more than three decades. In the fifth through seventh editions of  Manias, Panics and Crashes , Bob has in his turn made two major contributions. First, he has posed the question of how capital flows lead to manias and crashes, bringing in elements from the debate over German reparations after WWI. Second, he has posed the question of the link between successive waves of manias, including exchange rates and capital flows. The WWI version of the capital flow problem posed the question of how the payment of an indemnity by Germany to France could lead to more net exports from the payer and lower net exports from the receiver. Keynes’ polemical answer  in the  Economic Consequences of the Peace  centered on how much Germany’s prices would have to fall relative to those of its trading partners—by way of suggesting the impossibility or at least the harshness of the  reparations. Ohlin  ironically answered in a more Keynesian fashion using income changes. In particular, higher German taxes or lower German government expenditure, and the reverse in France, would affect incomes. Germans would reduce spending not only on exports and imports but also on home goods and services like haircuts and thereby release resources to produce more goods for export. The French would increase spending with the opposite effects. Aliber re-cast this so-called  transfer problem  into the question of how an economy responds not to official flows but to a big inflow of private capital. His answer is that it can set in motion a mania. It raises the prices of stocks and bonds, adding to private wealth. It can stimulate and fund bank lending and other credit creation, giving a particular lift to real estate prices. With a floating exchange rate, the capital inflow appreciates the exchange rate. If firms have borrowed in foreign currency, currency appreciation flatters their balance sheets, reducing debt relative to equity and increasing the supply of bank loans. All of these lead to greater domestic spending relative to domestic production and thereby a deterioration in external trade. The current account deteriorates to match the capital inflow. The transfer is made to happen not, as  with Ohlin’s  story, through changes in the government budget, but rather through the effect on private spending of easier credit, lower financing costs, higher wealth, and exchange rate appreciation. In this story, the exchange rate movements contribute to the unsustainable accumulation of debt rather than adjusting to maintain equilibrium, as foreseen by the proponents of floating exchange rates. When the capital inflow reverses, boom turns to bust. This view does not take it as a coincidence if several countries experience manias simultaneously. Rather, attention should be paid to similar inflows of capital. Tiny Iceland’s outsized equity bubble and deterioration of its trade accounts in the years before 2008 played an important role in clarifying these dynamics to Bob.  Michael Lewis 
 ’  Boomerang  recounts Bob’s 2006 prescient call that Iceland had passed the point of no return and would encounter a traumatic crash. 
 7 
  A friend quipped that just as Darwin had to go to the Galapagos Islands to grasp evolution, so Aliber had to go to Iceland to recognize the manic power of capital inflows with a floating exchange rate. The 7th edition’s epilogue on the Chinese real estate market proved timely and insightful when big Chinese real estate companies became distressed in the middle of 2021. It remains an epilogue in this edition, though the story is updated. Bob’s second major contribution is the question of how successive major manias in different countries since the 1970s are linked. His answer is that the outcome of the previous mania and crash unleash exchange rate changes and capital flows that set the stage for the next wave of crises. Charlie and Bob are tough acts to follow. My main contribution to this 8th edition is the new chapter on the lender of last resort in this century; the conclusion focuses on the same issue. Another new chapter concerns  the mania for cryptocurrencies , on the grounds that it is the most speculative asset ever invented by the human mind. My first stab at the topic within weeks of the November 2021 peak of crypto prices generated heavy web traffic, an appearance on CNBC, and not a little vitriol from crypto ‘bros’ on  Twitter . 
 8 
  By May 2022, my return to the same venue to describe crypto runs and collapses faced much more competition. 
 9

         1. Financial Crises: A Hardy Perennial

       When this work first appeared, it looked back a long way to the financial crisis of the 1930s and revived interest in an old theme. Few books on the subject appeared during the several decades after World War II, following the spate of the 1930s, because the industry that produces them is anticyclical in character, 1  and recessions from 1945 to 1973 were few, far between, and exceptionally mild. This work also looked forward, four years it turned out, to the developing country debt crisis of 1982. In the decades since, 1982 proved just the first of four waves of financial crises. Debtors in three, four, or more countries defaulted at about the same time and the prices of real estate and securities in these countries fell sharply. Each country that experienced a financial crisis also had a recession as household wealth declined in response to the sharp fall in the prices of securities and real estate, and as the banks became much more reluctant suppliers of credit as their own capital was depleted. The Great Recession that began in 2008 was the most severe and the most global since the Great Depression of the 1930s. The first wave of financial crises broke in the early 1980s when  Mexico, Brazil , Argentina, and other developing countries defaulted on hundreds of billions of US-dollar-denominated debt to international banks. The second wave occurred in the early 1990s and  engulfed Japan  and two of the Nordic countries—Finland and Sweden; Norway had had a similar crisis a few years earlier. The Asian Financial Crisis that began in mid-1997 was the third wave; initially, it hit  Thailand, Malaysia , and Indonesia and subsequently South Korea, Russia, Brazil, and Argentina. The financial crisis that hit Mexico during its presidential transition at the end of 1994 served in some ways a dress rehearsal for the crisis in Southeast Asia thirty months later. The fourth wave began in September 2008 with the failure of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the two large US-government-sponsored mortgage lenders and the collapse of Lehman Brothers a few days later; the debacle of these lenders followed a sharp decline in the price of US real estate that had started in 2006. Britain, Spain, Ireland, and Iceland also were involved in the fourth wave. Financial crises strike at the peaks of business cycles. We are not interested in the business cycle as such, the rhythm of economic expansion and contraction, but only in the financial crisis that is the culmination of a period of expansion and leads to  downturn. Raymond Goldsmith’s  pithy definition comes close: a financial crisis is ‘a sharp, brief, ultracyclical deterioration in all or most of a group of financial indicators – [private?] short-term interest rates, asset (stock, real estate, land) prices, commercial insolvencies and failures of financial institutions.’ 2  Business cycles without financial crises lie outside our interest. Isolated financial crises that prove so manageable as to have no effects on the economic system are also neglected to an extent. The financial crises we shall consider here are major both in size and in effect and, as a rule, international in scope. By no means does every upswing in business excess lead inevitably to mania and panic. But the pattern occurs sufficiently frequently and with sufficient uniformity to merit renewed study. What happens, basically, is that some event changes the economic outlook. New opportunities for profits are seized, and overdone, in ways so closely resembling irrationality as to constitute a mania. Investors and firms leverage their positions with borrowed money and credit expands rapidly. Once the excessive character of the upswing is realized, the financial system experiences a sort of ‘distress,’ in the course of which the rush to reverse the expansion process may become so precipitous as to resemble panic. In the manic phase, people of wealth or credit switch out of money or borrow to buy real or illiquid financial assets. In a panic, the reverse movement takes place, from real or financial assets to money, or repayment of debt, with a crash in the prices of commodities, houses, buildings, land, stocks, bonds—﻿in short, in whatever has been the subject of the mania. The issues to be probed are several. Are markets so rational that manias—irrational by definition—cannot occur? If, on the other hand, such manias do occur, should they be allowed to run their course without governmental or other authoritative interference—at the risk of financial crisis and even panic that may spread through propagation by one means or another to other financial markets at home and possibly abroad? Or is there a salutary role to be played by a ‘lender of last resort,’ who comes to the rescue and provides the public good of stability that the private market is unable to produce for itself? And if the services of a lender of last resort are provided nationally, by the government or by such official institutions as a central bank, what agency or agencies can furnish stability to the international system, for which no government exists? Charles Kindleberger’s  The World in Depression, 1929–1939  concluded that the 1930s depression was wide, deep, and prolonged because there was no international lender of last resort. 3  Britain was unable to act in that capacity because it was exhausted by World War I, obsessed with pegging the British pound to gold at its pre-1914 parity, and groggy from the aborted economic recovery of the early 1920s. The United States was unwilling to act as an international lender of last resort; few Americans had thought through what the United States might have done if it had chosen to take on that role. The present work started as an attempt to extend the analysis more widely in time and space. Speculative excess, referred to concisely as a mania, and revulsion from such excess in the form of a crisis, crash, or panic looks to be, if not inevitable, at least historically common. The four waves of crises of the last 40 years offer all too much evidence. During a crisis, many firms that recently appeared robust can suddenly become bankrupt because the failure of a few lenders leads to a withdrawal of  credit, fire sales  of securities, and a slowdown in the economy. When the prices of securities decline sharply, government intervention may be desirable to prevent the price changes from becoming self-justifying and thereby to provide the public good of stability. At such times a lender of last resort can provide financial stability or attenuate financial instability. The policy dilemma is that if investors know in advance that governmental support will be forthcoming at such times, they will be less cautious in their purchases of securities and crises might occur more frequently. The role of the lender of last resort in coping with a crash or panic is fraught with ambiguity and dilemma. Thomas Joplin commented on the behavior of the Bank of England in the crisis of 1825: ‘There are times when rules and precedents cannot be broken; others, when they cannot be adhered to with safety.’ 4  Breaking the rule establishes a precedent and a new rule that can be adhered to or broken as the occasion demands. In these circumstances, intervention is an art rather than a science. The general rules that the state should always intervene or that the state should never intervene are both wrong. This same question about the wisdom of intervention reappeared in the last century. Should the US government have rescued Chrysler in 1979? Should the State of New York have rescued New York City in 1975? Should the federal banking authorities have rescued Continental Illinois Bank in 1984? (Continental Illinois was nationalized, although the depositors, both insured and uninsured, in the bank were made whole.). Similarly, should the Bank of England have rescued Baring Brothers in 1995 after the rogue trader Nick Leeson in its Singapore branch office had depleted the firm’s capital through hidden transactions in option contracts? Should the International Monetary Fund have lent to  Mexico, Brazil , and Argentina in the 1980s, and Mexico, Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea, Brazil, and Russia in the 1990s? And the question reappeared in the present century. Should the Fed not have rescued Bear Stearns and AIG? Should the Fed have lent to Lehman Brothers? Should the Bank of England have intervened earlier in the run on Northern Rock? Should many governments have injected equity into many, many banks in 2008? The list of questions emphasizes that the problem of financial crisis is still very much with us. The monetary aspects of manias and panics are important and are examined at length in several chapters. The monetarist view—or at least one monetarist view—is that a mania would not occur if the rate of growth of the money supply were low and stable. (The twenty-first century version might be that the mania would not occur if the central bank sets policy interest rates according to an inflation-targeting Taylor rule linking policy to inflation and unemployment.) To be sure, banking crises in which monetary growth accelerates early or late in the process should be distinguished from those in which the growth in the money supply did not increase significantly. But in principle, this view overlooks the capacity of bank credit to grow rapidly on the basis of non-money liabilities, including domestic near money and cross-border wholesale funding. In particular, many surges in credit within economies draw on surges in cross-border inflows of funds. 5  And it overlooks the propensity of nonbank financial institutions to gain share in extending credit in a boom. And it overlooks the possibility of direct credit, whether vendor financing or peer-to-peer lending. In practice, the conventional monetary measure of M2 plus CDs did not flash a strong red signal during the bubble years of the late 1980s  in Japan . The rate of increase in US stock prices in the second half of the 1920s was exceptionally high relative to the rate of growth of the money supply, and similarly, the rate of increase in the prices of NASDAQ stocks in the second half of the 1990s was exceedingly high relative to the growth of the US money supply. The earliest manias discussed in the first edition of this book were the South Sea and Mississippi bubbles of 1719–1720. The earliest manias analyzed in this edition are the  Kipper- und Wipperzeit , a monetary crisis (1619–1622) that occurred at the outbreak of the Thirty Years War, and the much-discussed ‘tulipmania’ of 1636–1637. The early historical treatment focuses on European experiences. The most recent full-scale crises covered in this edition center on the real estate markets in the United States, Britain, Ireland, Spain, and Iceland that began in 2008. More recent events treated include the international lender of last resort in March 2020, and boom and distress if not bust in crypto assets and Chinese housing. The concentration on the financial crises in Britain in the nineteenth century reflects both the central importance of London in international financial arrangements and the abundant writings by contemporary analysts. In contrast, Amsterdam was the dominant financial power for much of the eighteenth century, but events there are slighted because of the difficulties in accessing the Dutch literature. The waves of surges in the supply of credit and the subsequent financial crises since the mid-1970s suggest that these market events have become more global than in the past. Most of the countries that have experienced surges in the supplies of credit that led to sharp increases in the prices of real estate and securities also experienced increases in cross-border investment inflows. These inflows led to increases in the prices of currencies unless they were anchored to parities and to increases in the prices of securities. Each country experienced an economic boom—‘the times could not be better.’ Perhaps because of the increases in the prices of currencies, the upward pressures on prices of goods have been smaller than they would have been had the currencies been pegged. Nevertheless, the central banks in many countries raised interest rates to dampen inflationary pressures due to the boom—which attracted more money from abroad. Technological innovations in communications and computing mean that the costs of cross-border investment inflows have declined; investors shift funds to a foreign center for a small anticipated incremental return. Moreover, there is a larger pool of liquid funds denominated in the US dollar in the offshore market that investors can tap when they want to buy securities and assets in countries whose financial and economic prospects suddenly look much brighter. The Story Chapter by Chapter Chapter  2  presents a stylized model of speculation, credit expansion, financial distress, and then crisis that ends in a panic and crash. The model follows the early classical ideas of ‘over-trading’ followed by ‘revulsion’ and ‘discredit’—musty terms used by earlier generations of economists including Adam Smith, John Stuart Mill, Knut Wicksell, and Irving Fisher. These concepts were developed further by Hyman Minsky, who argued that the US financial system is unstable, fragile, and prone to crisis. The Minsky model has great explanatory power for earlier crises in the United States and in Western Europe, for the surges in the prices of real estate and equities  in Japan  in the second half of the 1980s, and for the sharp increases in real estate prices in the United States, Britain, Ireland, Spain, and Iceland between 2002 and 2007. Each of these crises followed a surge in real estate prices that followed an increase in the supply of credit. The analysis itself, with copious historical illustrations, begins in Chapter  3  with its focus on speculation, the mania phase. The central issue is whether speculation can be destabilizing as well as stabilizing—whether, in other words, markets are always rational. Do investors in real estate and in stocks anticipate prices on the basis of recent increases in the prices of these assets—the bubble case—or do they anticipate prices on the basis of their estimates of their earning power? The nature of the outside, exogenous shock that triggers the mania is examined in different historical settings including the onset and the end of a war, a series of good harvests and a series of bad harvests, the opening of new markets and of new sources of supply and the development of different innovations—the railroad, electricity, the automobile, and the internet. A particular displacement that has shocked the system has been financial liberalization or deregulation  in Japan , the Nordic countries, some Asian countries, Mexico, Russia, and Iceland. Deregulation has led to both domestic credit expansion and to increases in borrowing in foreign centers to finance domestic loans and speculative investment. Ronald McKinnon and Edward Shaw condemned government restraints on banking as financial repression in the 1970s and many since have taken increases in the ratio of private credit to GDP as signs of increased welfare. 6 Investors have speculated in commodities, agricultural land, urban building sites, railroads, new banks, discount houses, stocks, bonds (both foreign and domestic), glamor stocks, conglomerates, condominiums, shopping centers, and office buildings. Moderate excesses burn themselves out without significant damage to the economy although individual investors encounter large losses. One question is whether the euphoria of the economic upswing endangers financial stability only if it involves at least two or more objects of speculation, a bad harvest, say, along with a railroad mania or an orgy of land speculation, or a bubble in real estate and in stocks at the same time. Chapter  4  analyzes the monetary dimensions of both manias and panics. On occasion a boom or a panic results from a monetary event—a recoinage, a discovery of precious metals, a change in the ratio of the price of gold to the price of silver under bimetallism, an unexpected success of some flotation of a stock or bond, a sharp reduction in interest rates as a result of a massive debt conversion, or a rapid expansion of the monetary base. Innovations in finance, as in productive processes, can shock the system and lead to overinvestment in some types of financial services, especially if competition and lack of experience lead innovations to be underpriced. 7  The financial sector expanded rapidly in the United States during its real estate boom because of the rapid increase in the demand for mortgages following the introduction of private-label mortgage-backed securities (MBSs) that sliced up claims to the interest income and the principal of a large number of mortgages that were held in a trust. The problems associated with managing the monetary mechanism to avoid manias and bubbles deserve stress. Many monetarists insist that many, perhaps most, of the cyclical difficulties of the past have resulted from mismanagement of the monetary mechanism. Such mistakes were frequent and serious. The argument advanced in Chapter  4 , however, is that even when the supply of money was adjusted to the economy’s demands, the financial system may proceed to produce many close substitutes for money, just as lawyers find new loopholes in tax laws as fast as legislation closes up the old ones. The evolution of money from coins to bank notes, bills of exchange, bank deposits, and finance paper illustrates the point. The Currency School may have been right about the need for a fixed supply of money, but it was wrong to believe that it could be achieved. Moreover, banks or nonbank lenders can access wholesale funding, especially from abroad, to fund credit extension. Then, credit to households and developers can grow faster than money and enable surges in the prices of real estate. Chapter  5  describes the crisis stage, with an emphasis on domestic aspects. One question is whether manias can be halted by official warnings—moral suasion or jawboning. By and large, the evidence suggests that they cannot, or at least that many crises followed warnings that were intended to head them off. One widely noted remark was that of Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, who stated on December 6, 1996, that he thought the New York stock market was ‘irrationally exuberant,’ This was at a time when the Dow Jones industrial average was 6400. It subsequently rose to over 11,000. The NASDAQ was 1300 at the time of the Greenspan remark and peaked at more than 5000 four years later. A similar warning had been issued in February 1929 by Paul M. Warburg, a private banker who was one of the fathers of the Federal Reserve system, without slowing the stock market’s upward climb. The nature of the event that ultimately produces a turning point is discussed: some bankruptcy, defalcation, or troubled area revealed or rumored, a sharp rise in the central bank discount rate to halt the hemorrhage of cash into domestic circulation or abroad. And then there is the interaction of falling prices—the crash—and its impact on the liquidity of the economy. Chapter  6  considers swindles and defalcations. Sometimes, the revelation of some misfeasance, malfeasance, or malversation (the corruption of officials) engendered during the mania precipitates a crash and panic. Other times the crash and panic reveal frauds and swindles that had proliferated in the froth of the mania. It seems clear from the historical record that swindles are a response to the greedy appetite for wealth stimulated by the boom: demand creates its own supply. Demand is strong:  short-seller Jim Chanos  claims that ‘we are in the golden age of fraud.’ 8  It is remarkable that recent corporate frauds,  including Theranos , a Silicon Valley startup whose young female founder promised a blood test based on drops of blood,  and Wirecard , a German company booking bogus profits from electronic payments, came to light in mid-boom. By contrast, the rogue’s gallery of corrupt business firms of the 1990s, Enron, MCIWorldCom, Tyco, Dynergy, and Adelphia were revealed after the crash of tech stocks in 2000. The regularity remains that the revelation of swindles occurs as a mania passes from euphoria to distress to crash. And as the monetary system gets stretched, institutions lose liquidity, and unsuccessful swindles are about to be revealed, the temptation to take the money and run becomes virtually irresistible. Chapter  7  deals with domestic propagation or contagion. It was mentioned just now that a financial crisis may be more serious if two or more, rather than just one, good or asset is the subject of speculation. History seems to show that a boom in one market spills over into others. When and if a crash comes, moreover, it may seize up the banking system and, quite apart from any change in the quantity of money, lead banks to ration credit all around. The connections between the stock and commodities markets were especially strong in New York in 1921 and 1929, and those linking shares and real estate again in 1929, and in 1987, and notably  in Japan  and the Nordic countries in 1988–1990. Chapter  8  traces the international contagion of manias and crises from the seventeenth to the first half of the twentieth century; two, three, four, or more countries experienced similar manias at the same time. There are two competing narratives. One invokes the metaphor of the sun and the moon, with the mania initiated in one country, often a large one, and then ‘beamed’ to its smaller neighbors or trading partners. An alternative posits that these countries are subject to the same displacement or innovation. Connections run through many linkages among countries, including trade, arbitrage of securities, capital flows, changes in central bank reserves of gold or foreign exchange, and direct contagion of speculators in euphoria or gloom. Some surges in the supply of credit are national, others global in that two, three, or more countries are involved. Some crises are national, others international. What constitutes the difference? Did, for example, the 1907 panic in New York precipitate the collapse of the Società Bancaria ltaliana via pressure on Paris communicated to Turin by withdrawals of bank deposits? There is a fundamental ambiguity here. Tight money in one financial center can serve either to attract funds or to repel them, depending on the expectations that a rise in interest rates generates. With inelastic expectations—no fear of crisis or that the price of the currency might decline—an increase in the discount rate attracts funds from abroad and helps provide the cash needed to ensure liquidity; with elastic expectations of changes—of falling prices, bankruptcies, or the decline in the price of the currency—raising the discount rate may suggest to foreigners the need to take more funds out rather than bring new funds in. The trouble is familiar in economic life generally. A rise in the price of a commodity may lead consumers to postpone purchases in anticipation of a decline or to speed up purchases before prices rise further. And even where expectations are inelastic, and the increase in the discount rate at the central bank sets in motion the right reactions, lags in responses may be so long that the crisis begins before the Marines arrive. One complex but not unusual trigger that leads to a financial crisis is a sudden halt to foreign lending, perhaps because of a domestic boom. Thus the boom in Germany and Austria in 1873 led to a decline in money outflows and contributed to the difficulties of Jay Cooke in the United States. Similar developments occurred with the Baring crisis in 1890, when troubles in Argentina led the British to halt lending  to South Africa , Australia , the United States, and the rest of Latin America. The stock market boom in New York in the spring of 1928 led Americans to cut off buying bonds of Germany and various Latin American countries, which in turn caused these countries to slide into depression. A halt to foreign trading is likely to precipitate depression abroad, which may in turn feed back to the country that launched the process. 9 The discussion in Chapter  9  takes up international contagion since the mid-twentieth century and highlights the four waves of banking crises since the early 1980s and the relationships among the successive waves. The likelihood that these four waves are independent and unrelated seems low. The first of these waves was preceded by the surge in bank loans to governments and government-owned firms in Mexico and other developing countries in the 1970s, and the second surge was in Tokyo in the second half of the 1980s; was there a connection between the developing country debt crisis and the surge in property prices in Japan? The third wave was in  Thailand, Malaysia , Indonesia, Russia, and other developing countries in the mid-1990s, while the fourth wave occurred in the real estate markets in the United States, Britain, Ireland, Iceland, and Spain ten years later. Surges in the prices of real estate cannot occur without the rapid growth of credit, either in the aggregate or to particular groups of borrowers. The theme of this chapter is that there was a systematic relationship among these waves, or at least between the first and the second, and the second and the third. The surge in the supply of credit to Mexico and other developing countries in the 1970s had responded to the growth of the offshore dollar market that took off when the United States and Germany set different interest rates in 1971. When these credit flows slowed sharply the prices of the currencies of these countries declined and the dollar rose. When the dollar fell after 1985, the Bank of Japan resisted the pressure toward the increase in the price of the yen in the second half of the 1980s amid deflation by lowering its interest rates and keeping them low. When property prices and stock prices  in Japan  began to decline at the beginning of the 1990s, the price of the yen increased and Japanese firms rapidly increased their investments in production facilities in Southeast Asia. The prices of the currencies of these countries increased unless they were prevented from doing so, and the prices of real estate increased. When stock prices and real estate prices in Bangkok and the other Asian capitals began to decline in 1997, the prices of the Asian currencies declined sharply, and there was a surge in the flow of money to New York as Asian borrowers repaid their foreign loans. Domestic crisis management is reviewed in Chapters  10  and  11 . The first of these two chapters considers the range of domestic responses to a crisis; at one extreme the government may take a hands-off approach, and at the other there is a range of miscellaneous measures. Those who believe that the market is rational and can take care of itself prefer the hands-off approach; according to one formulation, it is healthy for the economy to go through the purgative fires of deflation and bankruptcy to get rid of the mistakes and excesses of the boom. Among the miscellaneous devices are legal holidays, bank holidays, the issue of scrip, guarantees of liabilities, issuance of government debt,  deposit insurance , and the formation of special institutions like the Reconstruction Finance Corporation in the United States in 1932 and the Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale (IRI) in Italy in 1933. The Italian literature calls the process the ‘salvage’ of banks and companies; the British in 1974–1975 referred to saving the fringe banks as a ‘lifeboat’ operation. Chapter  11  addresses the policy choices related to a domestic lender of last resort—whether there should be such a lender, who this lender should be and how it should operate. A key topic is ‘moral hazard’—if market participants are confident that they will be ‘bailed out’ by a lender of last resort, their self-reliance is weakened. But on the other hand, policymakers may choose to halt the panic today rather than worry about the adverse effects on incentives tomorrow. If there is a lender of last resort, however, whom should it save? Insiders? Outsiders and insiders? Only the solvent, if illiquid? The distinction between solvent and insolvent firms depends on the scope and duration of the panic. These are political questions, and they are raised in particular when it becomes necessary to legislate to increase the capital of the deposit insurer when it runs out of funds to support banks in trouble in a time of acute stress. The issue was particularly acute in the 1990s  in Japan , where the collapse of the Nikkei stock bubble in 1990 uncovered all sorts of bad real estate loans by banks, credit unions, and other financial houses, confronting the government with the headache of deciding how much of a burden to put on the taxpayer. If the taxpayers didn’t take the hit, then the owners of bonds and stocks would incur very large losses because the prices of these securities would decline further. Particularly troubling in this context was the catatonic state of government in Japan in the 1990s—slow to decide how to meet the crisis and even slower to act. One of the key issues that a domestic lender of last resort must deal with is whether to extend credit to banks that may be insolvent. The Bagehot doctrine was that the lender of last resort should supply unlimited credit to illiquid but solvent institutions but not supply credit to an insolvent institution. Whether a bank is solvent depends on the prices of the securities and loans in its portfolio. During a crisis, cash is king, and the potential buyers of securities are hiding in the woodwork; a large decline in the prices of securities is necessary to induce them to part with cash. Even though the sale  occurred at fire-sale  prices, the banks that own these securities must use the sales price in valuing their own portfolios, even though these prices seem exceptionally low relative to the interest income on these securities. Chapter  12  discusses the role of the international lender of last resort in providing global monetary stability up until the end of the twentieth century. There was no responsible government or agency of government with the de jure responsibility for providing this public good of global monetary stability. The key question is where the international lending of last resort comes from. Before World War II, the central bank of the leading financial center of the world, often assisted by other countries, might play this role. But it might not, with adverse consequences. After World War II, a hybrid international lender of last resort emerged. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) was established as a treaty-based global organization to reduce the likelihood that countries would manage the prices of their currencies to secure a competitive advantage in the production of exports. It could lend to finance temporary deficits in international trade in goods and services, but its lending was by design slow, limited and conditional. It evolved from lending to countries trying to stabilize their currencies exchange rates through the 1970s to lending to developing countries trying to manage their external debts in the 1980s and 1990s. But leading central banks also continued to play a role. In the Latin American debt crisis of the 1980s, creditor country central banks helped to organize the rescheduling of private bank claims, and they returned to this role with South Korea in the Asian Financial Crisis. Starting in the early 1960s, major central banks agreed to provide each other with short-term credits known as swaps. These were extended for the short term, mostly to manage exchange rates, with the understanding that the borrower would refinance over the medium term with the IMF if necessary. In the 1980s and to a lesser extent in the 1990s, swaps were extended to some emerging market countries as ‘bridges’ to IMF borrowings. The international lender of last resort changed so much in the twenty-first century that it merits a separate Chapter  13  in this edition. Non-US banks suffered from a major loss of dollar funding in 2008 and again in 2020, and the Fed advanced dollars to a range of central banks that in turn provided them to banks in their home markets. What had only been a possibility since the inception of the swap lines in the early 1960s became a reality: the Fed offered swaps with no ex ante limits to its partner central banks. The object of the episode mixed strong, if often overlooked, self-interest—lowering key market rates that set debt-servicing costs for US firms and households—with service to the global good of financial stability—countering a run on non-US banks’ global dollar borrowing. Taking into account regional swaps extended in modest amounts by the ECB and  the Swiss National Bank , central banks, predominantly the Fed, had become the global lenders of last resort. This chapter also tells the story of the Fed as stabilizer of global dollar bond markets in early 2020. As  the COVID  pandemic broke out, panic selling of US  Treasury  and corporate  bonds  hit what is usually the world’s broadest, deepest, and most liquid bond market. Runs on bond mutual funds threatened a spiral of lower  prices and fire-sale  bond selling. The Fed’s response in buying US Treasury and even US corporate bonds did not just stabilize these markets, but also the $6 trillion market for dollar bonds issued by borrowers outside the US. However domestic its focus, the Fed brought stability not only to the global banking market but also to the global bond market. Chapter  14  profiles the mania in cryptocoins, coded anonymous money produced and traded privately over the internet. At a peak aggregate valuation of $3 trillion in November 2021, its sheer scale does not necessarily merit a chapter. But these assets soared in value while offering no cash flow, no ultimate redemption, little use value, and, for the largest, environmental damage. But crypto engages so intriguingly with so many of the themes of this book that it deserves consideration. More than anything, the judgment to buy them arose from the sight of friends (and more remote objects of comparison) getting rich overnight. The account here emphasizes the illusion of decentralization in crypto and asks what risks arise from its central institutions, including both trading platforms and its pseudo-money,  so-called stablecoins . While its anonymity and vulnerability attracted criminals and hackers, in the main crypto is not strictly a fraud. But its cash flows are often likened to those of a financial swindle, but the question is which kind of swindle bears the best likeness? Chapter  15  concludes. The lender of last resort should exist but its presence should be doubted. For example, uncertainty about whether New York City would be helped, and by whom, may have been the appropriate policy in the long run, so long as help was finally provided, and so long as there was doubt right to the end as to whether it would be forthcoming. This is a neat trick: eventually always come to the rescue, in order to prevent needless deflation, but always leave it uncertain whether rescue will arrive in time or at all, so as to instill caution in other speculators, banks, cities, or countries. In Voltaire’s  Candide , the head of a general was cut off ‘to encourage the others.’ A sleight of hand may be necessary to ‘encourage’ the others (without, of course, cutting off actual heads) not to anticipate the lender of last resort because the alternative of not providing it has such unhappy consequences for the economic system. An epilogue updated from the 7th edition focuses on the implosion of property prices and the decline in real estate construction that threatens the Chinese economy. The economic achievements of China since the early 1980s have been brilliant; three hundred to four hundred million have moved into the middle class, with clean water in and dirty water out. Property prices have soared and are extraordinarily high, and at the same time, there are thirty or fifty million empty apartments. The combination of high prices and empty apartments suggests the relevance of the quip of the great Yogi Berra: ‘It’s so expensive no one can afford to live there.’ Ponzi Finance, Chain Letters, Pyramid Schemes, Manias, and Bubbles Ponzi finance , chain letters, bubbles, pyramid schemes, and manias are somewhat overlapping terms for non-sustainable patterns of financial behavior, in that the prices of securities today are not consistent with the anticipated prices at distant future dates. Ponzi schemes generally involve promises to pay an interest rate of 30 or 40 or 50 percent a month; the entrepreneurs that develop these schemes always claim they have discovered a new secret formula so they can earn these high rates of return. They make the promised interest payments for the first few months with the money received from their new customers attracted by the promised high rates of return. But by the fourth or fifth month, the money received from these new customers is less than the monies promised to the first sets of customers and the entrepreneurs go  to Brazil  or jail or both. Bernie Madoff ran one of the largest Ponzi schemes ever, and his posted returns were in the range of ten to twelve percent—but steady. And he remained in business for more than fifteen years—probably long enough to merit the top position on the hit parade of longest-running Ponzi scheme. A chain letter is a particular form of pyramid arrangement; the procedure is that individuals receive a letter asking them to send $1 (or $10 or $100) to the name at the top of the pyramid and to send the same letter to five friends or acquaintances within five days; the promise is that within thirty days they will receive $64 for each $1 ‘investment.’ Pyramid arrangements often involve sharing of commission incomes from the sale of securities or cosmetics or food supplements by those who actually make the sales to those who have recruited them to become sales personnel. A bubble involves the purchase of an asset, usually real estate or a security, in anticipation that the asset or security can be sold to someone else at an even higher price; the term ‘the greater fool’ has been used to suggest the last buyer was always counting on finding someone else to whom the stock or the condo apartment or the baseball cards could be sold. The term ‘bubble’ suggests that when the prices stop increasing, they are likely—indeed almost certain—to decline. The term ‘mania’ describes the frenzied pattern of purchases, often an increase in prices accompanied by an increase in trading volumes; individuals are eager to buy before the prices increase further. Chain letters and pyramid schemes rarely have macroeconomic consequences, but rather involve isolated segments of the economy and involve the redistribution of income from the latecomers to those who were initially involved.
