       History vs. Economics Historians view each event as unique. In contrast, economists search for patterns in the flow of events, and for systematic relationships between an event and its antecedents. History is particular; economics is general. An economic model of a general financial crisis is presented in this chapter, while the phases of the speculative manias that eventually lead to crisis and collapse are set out in the following chapters. This model of a crisis covers only the boom and the subsequent bust and centers on the episodic nature of the mania and the subsequent events. Thus the model does not deal with the full turn of the business cycle. The business cycle is a standard feature of market economies; increases in investment spending lead to increases in household incomes and in GDP growth. Macroeconomics focuses on the explanations for the cyclical variations in the rates of growth of GDP around the long-run trend rates of growth and why these trend rates vary over time and place. The mania model also differs from models that focus on the periodicity of economic expansions and contractions, including the Kitchin inventory cycle of thirty-nine months, the Juglar cycle of investment in plant and equipment that has a periodicity of seven or eight years, and the Kuznets cycle of twenty years that highlights the rise and fall in housing construction. 1  The mania model is silent on the once regular, then ragged spacing of crises. In the first two-thirds of the nineteenth century, crises occurred regularly at ten-year intervals (1816, 1826, 1837, 1847, 1857, 1866), thereafter, less regularly (1873, 1907, 1921, 1929). Evidently, some time must elapse after one speculative mania that ends in crisis before investors have recovered sufficiently from their losses and disillusionment to be willing to take a flyer again. 
 The Model We start with the model of the late Hyman Minsky, a man with a reputation among monetary theorists for being particularly pessimistic, even lugubrious, in his emphasis on the fragility of the monetary system and its propensity to disaster. 2 Minsky highlighted that the changes in the supply of credit are pro-cyclical; the supply of credit increases when the economy is booming and decreases as the growth rate slows. Investors become more optimistic as an economy expands and they revise upward their estimates of the profitability of a wide range of investments, and they become more eager to borrow. At the same time, both the lenders’ assessments of the risks of individual investments and their risk averseness decline and they become more willing to make loans, including some for investments that they previously had deemed too risky. Eventually, debts weigh, the economy slows, and investors become less optimistic. The lenders also became more cautious as their loan losses increase, especially if these losses lead to declines in their capital. Although Minsky was a monetary theorist rather than an economic historian, his model lends itself effectively to the interpretation of economic and financial history. Indeed, in its emphasis on the instability of the credit system, it is a lineal descendant of a model, set out with personal variations, by a host of classical economists including John Stuart Mill, Alfred Marshall, Knut Wicksell, and Irving Fisher. Like Fisher, Minsky attached great importance to the role of debt structures in causing financial difficulties, and especially debt contracted to leverage the acquisition of speculative assets for subsequent resale. Financial economists are working to render aspects of Minsky’s model into formal, mathematical models. 3 Minsky’s Three-Part Taxonomy of Finance Minsky distinguished among hedge finance, speculative finance, and Ponzi finance—on the basis of the relation between the operating income of individual firms and their debt service payments. A firm is in the hedge finance group if its anticipated operating income is more than sufficient to pay both the interest and the scheduled reduction in its indebtedness. A firm is in the speculative finance group if its anticipated operating income is sufficient to pay the interest on its indebtedness; however, the firm must use cash from new loans to pay part or all of the amounts due on maturing loans. A firm is in the Ponzi group if its anticipated operating income is smaller than the amount needed to pay all of the interest on its indebtedness on the scheduled due dates, so the firm must either increase its indebtedness or sell some assets to get the cash for these interest payments. Minsky hypothesizes that the longer an economic upturn continues the more firms that had been in the hedge finance group move to the speculative finance group and the more firms that had been in this latter group move to the Ponzi finance group. Good economic times reward firms that adopt fragile financial structures; their growth leads to aggregate financial instability. Minsky’s use of the term ‘Ponzi finance’ memorializes Carlo Ponzi, who operated a small ‘near bank’ or deposit-taking firm, in a Boston suburb in the early 1920s. Ponzi promised to pay interest on the firm’s IOUs at the rate of 30 percent a month and his financial transactions went smoothly for three months. In the fourth month, however, the inflow of cash from new depositors was smaller than the interest payments promised to the older depositors and soon Ponzi was on his way to prison. Ponzi finance is now a generic term for a non-sustainable pattern of finance. The borrowers can only meet their commitments to pay the high interest rates on their outstanding loans if they can obtain cash from new loans. Initially many of the depositors are so pleased with their high rates of return that they allow their interest income to compound; the cliché is that they are ‘earning interest on the interest.’ Since in many Ponzi schemes, the interest rates are very high, often 30–40 percent a year, the continuation of the arrangement requires a continuous inflow of new money and often at an accelerating rate. The arrangement can operate only as long as the cash withdrawals are smaller than the inflow of new money. According to Minsky, events leading up to a crisis start with a  displacement , some exogenous, outside shock to the macroeconomic system. The nature of this displacement varies from one speculative boom to another. It may be the outbreak or end of a war, a bumper harvest or crop failure, the widespread adoption of an invention with pervasive effects—canals, railroads, the automobile, information technology, and the internet—some political event or surprising financial success, or a debt conversion that precipitously lowers interest rates. Financial liberalization has in various places opened up the credit taps and set off a speculative boom. An unanticipated change of monetary policy might constitute such a displacement. But whatever the source of the displacement, if it is sufficiently large and pervasive, it will alter the economic outlook by changing profit opportunities in at least one important sector of the economy. Displacement brings opportunities for profit in some new or existing lines and closes out others. As a result, business firms and individuals with savings or credit seek to take advantage of the former and retreat from the latter. If the new opportunities dominate those that lose, investment, and production pick up. A boom is under way. In Minsky’s model, the boom is fed by an expansion of bank credit that enlarges the total money supply. Banks typically can expand money, whether by the issue of bank notes under earlier institutional arrangements or by lending through an addition to the borrower’s deposit account. Bank credit is, or at least has been, notoriously unstable, with banks easing conditions in the upswing and tightening in the downswing, and the Minsky model rests squarely on that fact. This feature of the Minsky model is incorporated in what follows, but we go further. Before banks had evolved, and afterward, additional means of payment to fuel a speculative mania were available in the virtually infinitely expansible nature of personal credit and vendor finance. For a given banking system at a given time, monetary means of payment may be expanded not only within the existing system of banks but also by the formation of new banks, the development of new credit instruments, and the expansion of personal credit outside of banks. Crucial questions of policy turn on how to control all these avenues of monetary expansion. But even if the instability of old and potential new banks were corrected, instability of personal credit would remain to provide means of payment to finance the boom, given a sufficiently strong stimulus. Let us assume, then, that the urge to speculate is present and is transmuted into effective demand for goods or financial assets. After a time, increased demand presses against the capacity to produce goods or the supply of existing financial assets. Prices increase, giving rise to new profit opportunities and attracting still further firms and investors. Positive feedback develops, as new investment leads to increases in income that stimulate further investment and further income increases. At this stage, we may get what Minsky called  euphoria . Speculation for price increases is added to investment for production and sale. If this process builds up, the result is often, though not inevitably, what Adam Smith and his contemporaries called ‘overtrading.’ Now, overtrading is by no means a clear concept. It may involve pure speculation for a price rise, an overestimate of prospective returns, or excessive ‘gearing’ (or leverage, or borrowing against assets). 4  Pure speculation, of course, involves buying for resale rather than use in the case of commodities or for resale rather than income in the case of financial assets. Overestimation of profits comes from euphoria, affects firms engaged in productive and distributive processes, and requires no explanation. Excessive gearing arises from cash requirements that are low relative both to the prevailing price of a good or asset and to possible changes in its price. It means buying on margin, or by installments, under circumstances in which one can sell the asset and transfer with it the obligation to make future payments. As firms or households see others making profits from speculative purchases and resales, they tend to follow: ‘There is nothing so disturbing to one’s well-being and judgment as to see a friend get rich.’ 5  Similarly, banks may increase their loans because they are reluctant to lose market share to other lenders and to show lower profit growth. When the number of firms and households indulging in these practices grows large, bringing in segments of the population that are normally aloof from such ventures, speculation for profit leads away from normal, rational behavior to what has been described as a  mania  or  bubble . The word mania emphasizes the irrationality; bubble foreshadows the bursting. In the technical language of some economists, a bubble is any deviation from ‘fundamentals,’ whether up or down, leading to the possibility and even the reality of negative bubbles, which rather gets away from the thrust of the metaphor. More often small price variations about fundamental values (as prices) are called ‘noise.’ In this book, a bubble is an upward price movement over an extended range that then implodes. Investors’ forecasts of the price of an asset,  whether stocks, property, or cryptocurrency , on Friday, are based on the increase in its price from Monday to Thursday. An extended negative bubble is a crash. As we shall see in the next chapter, the object of speculation may vary widely from one mania or bubble to the next. It may involve primary products, especially those imported from afar (where the exact conditions of supply and demand are not known in detail), or goods manufactured for export to distant markets, domestic and foreign securities of various kinds, contracts to buy or sell goods or securities, land in the country or city, houses, office buildings, shopping centers, condominiums, and foreign exchange. At a late stage, speculation tends to detach itself from really valuable objects and turn to delusive ones. A larger and larger group of people seeks to become rich without a real understanding of the processes involved. Not surprisingly, swindlers and catchpenny schemes flourish. Although Minsky’s model focuses on the pro-cyclical changes in the supply of credit in a single country, overtrading has historically tended to spread from one country to another. The conduits are many. Internationally traded commodities and assets that go up in price in one market will rise in others through arbitrage. The foreign-trade multiplier communicates surging income in a given country to others through increased imports. For instance, the bubble  in Japan  in the 1980s had significant impacts on South Korea and Taiwan, because the firms in these economies were links in the Japanese supply chain and exported to firms in Japan; when Japan experienced a high rate of growth, South Korea and Taiwan also had high growth rates. Capital flows constitute a third link. Money flows of gold, silver (under the gold standard or bimetallism), or foreign exchange are a fourth. And there are purely psychological connections, as when investor euphoria or pessimism in one country infects investors in others. The declines in prices on October 24 and 29, 1929, and October 19, 1987, were practically instantaneous in all financial markets (except Japan), far faster than can be accounted for by arbitrage, income changes, capital flows, or money movements. Credit expansion in a booming country may be echoed abroad, even though in an ideal gold standard world, a gain of specie for one country would be matched by a corresponding loss for another, so that the resulting expansion in money and credit in the first case would be offset by the contraction in the second. In the real world, however, while the boom in the first country may gain speed from the increase in the supply of reserves, or ‘high-powered money,’ credit may also rise in the second despite the loss in monetary reserves, as investors respond to rising prices and profits abroad by joining in the speculative chase. In other words, the potential contraction from the shrinkage on the monetary side may be overwhelmed by the increase in speculative interest and the rise in demand. For the two countries together, in any event, the credit system is stretched tighter. As the speculative boom continues, interest rates, the velocity of circulation, and prices all continue to mount. At some stage, a few insiders decide to take their profits and sell out. At the top of the market, there is hesitation, as new recruits to speculation are balanced by insiders who withdraw. Prices begin to level off. There may then ensue an uneasy period of  financial distress . The term comes from corporate finance, where a firm is said to be in financial distress when it must contemplate the possibility, perhaps only a remote one, that it will not be able to meet its liabilities. For an economy as a whole, the equivalent is the awareness on the part of a considerable segment of the speculating community that a rush for liquidity—to get out of other assets and into money—may develop, with disastrous consequences for the prices of goods and securities, and leaving some speculative borrowers unable to pay off their loans. As distress persists, speculators realize, gradually or suddenly, that the market cannot go higher. It is time to withdraw. The race out of real or long-term financial assets and into money may turn into a stampede. The specific signal that precipitates the crisis may be the failure of a bank or firm stretched too tight, the revelation of a swindle or defalcation by someone who sought to escape distress by dishonest means, or a fall in the price of the primary object of speculation as it, at first alone, is seen to be overpriced. In any case, the rush is on. Prices decline. Bankruptcies increase. Liquidation sometimes is orderly but may degenerate into panic as the realization spreads that there is only so much money, not enough to enable everyone to sell out at the top. The word for this state—again, not from Minsky—is revulsion. Revulsion against commodities or securities leads banks to cease lending on the collateral of such assets. In the early nineteenth century, this condition was known as discredit. Overtrading, revulsion, and discredit—all these terms have a musty, old-fashioned flavor. They are imprecise, but they do convey a vivid story. Revulsion and discredit may go so far as to lead to panic (or as the Germans put it, Torschlusspanik, ‘door-shut-panic’), with people crowding to get through the door before it slams shut. The panic feeds on itself, as did the speculation, until one or more of three things happen: (1) prices fall so low that people are again tempted to move back into less liquid assets; (2) trade is cut off by setting limits on price declines, shutting down exchanges, or otherwise closing trading; or (3) a lender of last resort succeeds in convincing the market that money will be made available in sufficient volume to meet the demand for cash. Confidence may be restored even if a large volume of money is not issued against other assets; the mere knowledge that one can get money is frequently sufficient to moderate or even to eliminate the demand. Whether there should be a lender of last resort is a matter of some debate. Those who oppose the function argue that it encourages speculation in the first place. Supporters worry more about the current crisis than about forestalling some future one. There is also a question of the place for an international lender of last resort. In domestic crises, government or the central bank (when there is one) has responsibility. At the international level, there is neither a world government nor any world bank adequately equipped to serve as a lender of last resort. Central banks providing short-term credits to each other have shown themselves capable of discharging the role, but can they keep doing so? Dilemmas, debates, doubts, and questions abound. We shall have more to say about these questions later on. The Psychology of Ponzi Schemes and Market Manias By Clark McCauley* It is easy to suppose that greed is  the explanation for manias and Ponzi schemes , with panics and crashes the sad but inevitable result. Greed, according to Merriam-Webster, is an intense and selfish desire for something. Surely it must be greed that pushes people into the latest fad investment. Greed is not only selfish but solitary: Silas Marner, communing with his gold coins by candlelight, or Scrooge McDuck, dancing alone in his vault under a shower of cash. Kindleberger had a different idea: ‘There is nothing so disturbing to one’s well-being and judgment as to see a friend get rich.’ This well-polished line reliably elicited a nervous laugh from his audiences. The insight here is that manias are not the result of greed but of fear—the fear of falling behind. The psychology at the bottom of this fear  is social comparison theory —the idea that humans are driven to evaluate themselves by comparison with  others. FOMO (fear of missing out ) is more accurately seen as FOFB (fear of falling behind). Most of us do not aspire to be the world’s richest; we just don’t want to fall behind friends, relatives, neighbors, and co-workers. We want to keep up with the Joneses. Investing in a Ponzi scheme or market mania is not an individual failure reflecting an individual character flaw like greed. Rather it reflects the fact that humans are social creatures: we care about others and care how we compare with others. Kindleberger refers to the effect of watching a friend get rich—a motivating comparison to the extent that we are falling behind. But comparison extends beyond friends. Comparison can occur across generations: it is disturbing if we do not do as well as our parents. Comparison also occurs over time, within one person’s experience: it is disturbing to see yourself poorer today than you were five years ago. Motivating comparison is only half the story of Ponzi frauds. The other element is trust. Trust is a reciprocal expectation: you trust them to look out for you, and they trust you to look out for them. The importance of trust comes through in the prevalence of  affinity frauds  in Ponzi schemes. In a landmark study,  the  Marquet Report on Ponzi Schemes  reviewed 329 Ponzi cases revealed between 2002 and 2011.** Nearly one in four Ponzi schemes was an affinity fraud—a group with ingroup trust scammed by a member or supposed member of the ingroup. Eighty-five percent of affinity group frauds targeted an ethnic, religious, or elderly/retired group. Ingroup identity brings ingroup trust to the scammer. For the three quarters of the  Marquet Report  Ponzi schemes that were not affinity frauds, trust had to come from something other than ethnicity, religion, or age. Most likely it was trust in family or friends. Family and friends constitute a personal rather than demographic identity group, a personalized affinity group. Trust in family and friends in this network is likely greater than trust in a demographic identity, and the Ponzi power of family and friends is thus greater than the power of an affinity group. A market mania or bubble can be understood as a naturally occurring Ponzi—a boom and bust with no Charles Ponzi at the center of it. The motive is the same kind of social comparison that powers a Ponzi—fear of falling behind. But comparisons in a mania are less about personal contact and more about mass media, which in recent years means not only journalistic news sources but also web sites such  as Facebook , Twitter   and Redditt . In the US today, there is a sociological form of motivating comparison—between the rich and the rest. Wealth inequality in the United States has been increasing since 1990. In March 2022, the top ten percent of US households had about 70 percent of the wealth; the bottom fifty percent had 3 percent.*** The result of increasing inequality has been to focus more attention on wealth, strengthen stereotypes of the rich and the rest, and enhance ‘us’ versus ‘them’ comparisons of the rich and the rest.****  When Bill Gates   (Microsoft ), Mark Zuckerberg   (Facebook ),  and Jeff Bezos  (Amazon) are summoned to testify in Washington, they become targets of motivational comparison; they have grown richer as most Americans became (relatively) poorer. They also become advertisements for risky investment. What price/earnings ratio would have been too high to get in on the ground floor with these corporate heroes? For many Americans, a risky investment looks like a lottery ticket—the only chance to avoid falling behind. The stock market can look to non-experts like a lottery. Suppose I am looking at a rising market. The market may be the whole S&P 500, or a sector like the NASDAQ, or a particular stock  like Tesla . Should I invest? Should I buy a ticket? The first argument for investing is that many others have, enough others to produce the rising market. If they trusted this investment, I can. And they have made big money with this investment. I am falling behind those who have already invested. Of course, the market could go down. So there are four possibilities. I invest, the market continues up, and I am no longer falling behind. Or I invest, the market goes down. I am still not falling behind, my rank in the order of wealth stays the same. Or I don’t invest, the market continues up, and I fall further behind. ( Have fun staying poor!  is the crypto jibe.) Or I don’t invest, the market goes down, and I move ahead in the order of wealth. This gain is undermined, however, by the fact that my dollar wealth has not increased. Looking at the four outcomes, I am much better off investing if the market continues up. I am better off not investing if the market goes down, but I only feel slightly better because my money value is unchanged. Balancing these possibilities, I am likely to follow the crowd into the rising market. A further consideration is that there is no reason to think the market will go down. When the market is up, pundits, politicians, and economists compete for the news hole in which to explain WHY it is going up. There is much less space for those who might explain why the market is likely to go down next month. The result is that when the market is rising, most stories will explain why it is rising. Most of these explanations will have time signatures that predict further rise on top of the current rise being explained. So why do Ponzi frauds and no-fraud manias keep happening? Because we humans care about others (trust), and care how we are doing in relation to others (social comparison). All that is required to shut down manias and Ponzi schemes is to shut down trust and social comparison, and look out for number one. * Emeritus Professor of Social Psychology, Bryn Mawr College ** Marquet International,  The Marquet Report on Ponzi Schemes: A White Collar Fraud Study of Major Ponzi-Type Investment Fraud Cases Revealed from 2002 to 2011 , June 2, 2011,  http://​media.​cleveland.​com/​business_​impact/​other/​marquet_​report_​on_​ponzi_​schemes.​pdf , accessed June 18, 2022. ***  https://​www.​federalreserve.​gov/​releases/​z1/​dataviz/​dfa/​distribute/​chart/​#quarter:​130;series:​Net%20​worth;demographic:​networth;population:​1,3,5,7;units:​shares;range:​1989.​3,2022.​1 , accessed June 23, 2022. **** Jolanda Jetten, Kim Peters, Belén Álvarez, Bruno Gabriel Salvador Casara, Michael Dare, Kelly Kirkland, Ángel Sánchez-Rodríguez, Hema Preya Selvanathan, Stefanie Sprong, Porntida Tanjitpiyanond, Zhechen Wang, and Frank Mols, ‘Consequences of Economic Inequality for the Social and Political Vitality of Society: A Social Identity Analysis’,  Political Psychology , vol. 42, issue 1, December 2021, pp. 241–266. 
 The Validity of the Model Three criticisms have been directed at the Minsky model. One is that each crisis is unique, so a general model is misplaced. A second is that changes in the economic environment mean that this type of model is no longer relevant. A third is that asset price bubbles are highly improbable because ‘all the information is in the price’ and this price reflects the fundamentals—the mantra of the efficient-market view of finance. The first criticism is that each crisis is the product of a unique set of circumstances, or that there are such wide differences among financial crises that they should be arranged into various species, each with its own particular features. Banking crises were frequent in the first two-thirds of the nineteenth century and in the last third of the twentieth century. In this view, each crisis is unique and a product of a specific series of historical accidents—which was said about 1848 and about 1929, 6  and may be inferred from the historical accounts of separate crises noted throughout this book. Each crisis also has its unique individual features—the nature of the shock, the object of speculation, the form of credit expansion, the ingenuity of the swindlers and the nature of the incident that touches off revulsion. But if one may borrow a French phrase, the more something changes, the more it remains the same. Details proliferate; structure abides. Virtually every banking crisis has followed two, three, or more years when the rates of growth of the borrowers’ indebtedness exceeded 10 or even 20 percent a year—rates of growth that were too high to be sustained for an extended period. More compelling is the suggestion that the genus ‘crises’ should be divided into commercial, industrial, monetary, banking, fiscal, and financial (in the sense of financial markets) sub-species or into local, regional, national, and international groups. A large number of taxonomies can follow from this suggestion. A taxonomic approach is not accepted in this book because the primary concern is with international financial crises that involve a number of critical elements—speculation, increase in the supply of credit and borrowers’ indebtedness, rise in asset prices followed by a sharp fall, and rush into money. The test is whether the Minsky model provides insights about the broad features of crises. The second criticism is that the Minsky model of the instability of the supply of credit is no longer relevant because of structural changes in the institutional features of the economy, including the rise of large corporations and of big labor unions and big governments, modern banking, and speedier communications. Alvin Hansen claimed that something akin to the Minsky model applied satisfactorily to the world economy prior to the middle of the nineteenth century but then ceased to apply because the institutional structure underwent a sea change. Theories based on uncertainty of the market, on speculation in commodities, on ‘overtrading’, on the excesses of bank credit, on the psychology of traders and merchants, did indeed reasonably fit the early ‘mercantile’ or commercial phase of modern capitalism. But as the nineteenth century wore on, captains of industry... became the main outlets for funds seeking a profitable return through savings and investments. 7 
 Hansen—who was a foremost expositor of the Keynesian model of the business cycle and especially of the recently re-invoked risk of persistently high levels of unemployment amounting to ‘secular stagnation’—wanted to downplay the significance of any explanations for declines in economic activity other than increases in household or business saving. However, Hansen’s emphasis on the importance of the relationship between savings and investment does not require the rejection of the view that changes in the supply of credit and the extent of leveraged speculation can have important impacts on the prices of securities and the level of economic activity. The financial debacles in  Mexico, Brazil , Argentina, and more than ten other developing countries in the early 1980s are consistent with the Minsky model and his notion of Ponzi finance (see Box above); the external indebtedness of these countries increased much more rapidly than their interest payments on their loans in a pattern that could not be sustained. The surges in real estate prices and stock prices  in Japan  in the second half of the 1980s and the subsequent sharp declines in these prices are also consistent with the Minsky model. The booms and the subsequent busts in the second half of the 1990s in Thailand, Indonesia and Korea and then in Russia feature the same pattern of cash flows; initially the borrowers’ indebtedness increased much more rapidly than their interest payments on the indebtedness. The third criticism is that bubbles are impossible because market prices always reflect the economic fundamentals, and that sharp declines in the prices of securities usually reflect ‘policy switching’ by governments or central banks. Those who take this position dismiss the possibility that the surges in the prices of securities are the result of herd behavior, positive feedback, or bandwagon effects—credulous suckers following smart insiders. These critics suggest instead that the model is ‘mis-specified,’ that is, that something was going on and not taken into account by the theory, and that more research is needed. 8  Some of the research that these critics want is offered in this book. 
 The Relevance of the Minsky Model in the Twenty-First Century The Minsky model readily applies to the US real estate mania in the first decade of the twenty-first century that culminated in the Great Financial Crisis, which involved Iceland (see Box below), Spain, Ireland and others. The US displacement around the turn of the century was the private securitization of home mortgages. Securities that bundled mortgages guaranteed by the government or its agencies had been around for decades, and techniques for slicing cash flows to create ‘tranches’ with different exposures to the risk that homeowners would repay the mortgage early were also well developed. What was new was that bankers bundled together mortgages without a government guarantee and used the slicing technique to concentrate the resulting credit risk of homeowners defaulting in some tranches, leaving others able to make full payments in all but the most dire Great Depression-type scenarios. Thus, a given bundle of mortgages could give rise to ‘collateralised mortgage obligations’ or ‘collateralised debt obligations’ carrying a mix of mostly top investment grade ratings underpinned by securities carrying bottom junk bond ratings. This innovation increased the amount of money available for mortgages and propelled US house prices upward. Private mortgages could offer less money down than the government agencies had demanded to extend their guarantees, and loan to value ratios on the privately securitized mortgages rose toward 100 percent. Often mortgages that had qualified for government guarantees were refinanced with high leverage, allowing households to extract equity in a rising market. Or, households traded up to bigger houses, stretching to afford them with the help of low down payments and adjustable-rate mortgages. These could carry low ‘teaser’ rates for the first two years, by which time continued house price appreciation promised to make a new refinancing possible. The very predictability of the Fed’s interest rate hikes allowed mortgage bankers to count the cost of the teaser rates and undermined the rate hikes’ power to restrain. The boom of the early 2000s turned to euphoria in 2005–2006. The share of mortgages extended without government guarantees and with easy down payments reached a high level of 55 percent. Adjustable-rate mortgages—most priced off of the London interbank rate, Libor—amounted to 62 percent of private label mortgage-backed securities. 9 Lower down payments and rising house prices piled debt onto household balance sheets.  The Case-Shiller  index of house prices rose 93 percent from the beginning of 2000 to the peak in the first quarter of 2006 at a time of low overall inflation. Prices more than doubled in the hot markets responsible for disproportionate growth of mortgage debt. The ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 71 percent in 2000 to 99 percent in 2007. 10 Leverage rose not only in the mortgage  instrument  and in the household  sector , but also in  financial institutions , both large banks and securities dealers. US banks were constrained by a simple leverage ratio, so they used the wheeze of special-purpose investment vehicles to fund and to hold mortgage securities off their balance sheets. US securities firms faced no such constraints and piled 40 or 50 or so dollars of debt on each dollar of equity. So did major banks headquartered outside of North America, likewise unconstrained by any limit on overall leverage. As home prices rose, so did investment in housing. Sales of new single-family homes rose from a peak annual rate of less than a million in the previous cycle to a peak near 1.4 million in July of 2005. 11  Even with the boom in house prices with  the Covid  pandemic, sales have not sustained a rate of a million a year since then. The boom drew strength from international propagation, discussed further in Chapter  9 , which took place on balance sheets in the United States and spanning the Atlantic. Non-US banks were key players in the process from producing private mortgage-backed securities to the holding of them. Foreign banks’ US securities affiliates ranked high among underwriters and when top-rated insurer AIG stopped guaranteeing the top-rated securities, foreign banks ‘ate their own cooking’ and held them on their US balance sheets. European banks’ credit also took a round trip across the Atlantic: they borrowed from US money market funds, shipped the dollars to Europe, and funded holdings there of private mortgage-backed securities. And European banks borrowed dollars offshore to fund the securities. Adding it all up, foreign nationals ended up holding an estimated 40 percent of the private mortgage-backed securities with European banks doing the heavy lifting. After house prices peaked in 2006, distress arrived in the summer of 2007. Two Bear Stearns mortgage-backed securities funds blew up in June. In  August BNP Paribas  suspended redemptions of its euro-denominated funds invested in US mortgage securities because it could not obtain prices for them. October 2007 saw the peak of stock prices. Distress persisted for over a year. ‘Rather like a brontosaurus that has been bitten on the tail and most of the body hasn’t noticed yet, the signal is working its way up the vertebrae,’ observed  investor Jeremy Grantham  in July 2007. 12 The Minsky moment , or panic, arrived with the failure of Lehman Brothers in mid-September 2008. Officials responded with lending of last resort at the domestic and international levels. Chapter  13  highlights the breakthrough in the international lender of last resort in 2008. Often overlooked, the Fed entered the market for short-term private securities as buyer of  last resort  in 2008. In doing so, it set a precedent for last resort buying of corporate  bonds  in March 2020 that in the event gave support to dollar bonds issued by borrowers from all over the world. In 2008, governments injected equity into many banks and guaranteed bank borrowing. Crash was averted at the expense of unprecedented government intervention in a broad swathe of economies. So the Minsky model has proven its worth once in this century by drawing attention to the phased links among leverage, asset prices and real activity in the Great Financial Crisis. By 2022, was another proof on its way? In early 2022, the Fed belatedly began to reverse the monetary expansion that fueled what some consider the fifth great modern bubble following the United States in  1929, Japan  in 1989, the dot.coms in 2000 and the Great Financial Crisis in 2008. Equity,  housing and bond prices—and cryptocurrencies  in the fringes—all reached high levels in late 2021. The argument that high bond prices (low bond yields) justified high equity prices recalled the University of Tokyo professors’ argument that high Japanese property prices in 1989 justified high equity prices. Yet from the Minsky perspective, indicators of private indebtedness sent mixed signals. During the pandemic, US households used government transfers to pay down credit card debt and to stash an untidy sum in banks. The ratio of US corporate debt to GDP remained on its long-term trend, and corporate rating upgrades well exceeded downgrades into 2022. Bank solvency seemed strong. Nevertheless, the supply of credit was abundant, with private equity operators able to leverage up companies with a free hand to which the corporate raiders of the late 1980s only aspired. Likewise the composition of junk bonds had never been so skewed to the junkiest. One risk that is not captured in debt indicators is that investors and nonbank financial institutions jointly behave as if they were leveraged. If investors in bond funds sell their shares when bond prices decline, then the bond funds must dump bonds into a declining market. Securities markets rather than banks can suffer runs that seize up the credit mechanism. It would be a mistake to assume that the Great Financial Crisis is the twenty-first century’s last demonstration of the relevance of the Minsky model. The Saga of Iceland’s ‘Perfect’ Bubble Iceland is the smallest advanced economy—370,000 people—with its own currency. Between 2002 and 2007, prices of residential real estate doubled, which was not exceptional, while the prices of stocks increased by a factor of nine, which was exceptional. In 2002, the value of the assets owned by the three Icelandic banks was 150 percent of the country’s GDP, while in 2007 the value of these assets was eight times Iceland’s GDP. Moreover, Iceland’s GDP in 2007 was 20 percent larger than in 2002. Iceland’s banks were the most rapidly growing banks in the world. And then in September 2008 stock prices declined by 90 percent; the prices of real estate tumbled; the market for  the Icelandic krona  outside of central bank transactions disappeared; and the economy went into a recession—severe by Iceland’s standards but modest by those of other countries. Because Iceland is so small, the financial processes associated with a bubble are more readily visible than in larger countries. The saga began in 1998 when a market-oriented government began to privatize the three main banks, a process that was completed in 2003. The buyers of the shares and the new owners of the banks were politically connected businessmen; in one case the purchase of one of the privatized banks was financed by another bank. In 2002, the price of  the Icelandic krona  began to increase in response to three inflows of money. First, Icelandic banks marketed foreign currency loans to businesses in Iceland, which could seemingly profit from lower interest rates abroad. Eventually 80 percent of business loans were foreign currency denominated; as the kroner appreciated, firms’ balance sheets strengthened, their profits rose and banks increased the supply of credit. In addition, 20 percent of household debt came to be denominated in foreign currency, mostly auto loans but also some mortgages. With the supply of bank credit increasing, business and household debt rose rapidly. Second, some foreign investors bought Icelandic securities, looking for both an interest rate pickup (‘carry’) and exchange rate gains. The flow of money to Iceland was part of an increase in investment inflows to the United States, Britain, Ireland,  Spain, South Africa ,  and Australia . Third, the Icelandic banks in various ways lent in foreign currency for the purchase of Icelandic stocks, including their own shares. One wheeze was the banks’ lending to their own offshore affiliates to buy bank shares; another was loans to insiders to buy bank shares. All three of these inflows of money pushed up the exchange value of the krona and share prices. Since banks owned large amounts of the stocks of Icelandic firms, their profits and capital rose. And, as described, the banks were making sure that their own share prices were rising. Stock prices were increasing by 65–70 percent a year, and bank capital was increasing at the same rate. With household wealth rising and the krona strengthening, consumption and imports increased despite the interest rate hikes of the central bank. These hikes, of course, only increased the incentives for residents to borrow foreign currency and for global investors to hold krona. Iceland’s trade balance morphed from a small surplus to a deficit of nearly 20 percent of its GDP. The external indebtedness of Iceland exploded. The flow of money to Iceland was a multiple of the interest payments of the Icelandic residents to their foreign creditors. The newly privatized Icelandic banks sold their own IOUs to banks in London and Frankfurt and other foreign banking centers in order to fund their foreign currency loans to Icelandic firms and households. They traded on the country’s high rating and faced an elastic supply of interbank funding, especially from German banks. As Icelandic banks’ equity grew rapidly, the world was their oyster. They borrowed even more from banks to fund the purchase of high street stores in London and Copenhagen. The banks increased their loans at a pace that was almost as rapid as the increase in their capital. In 2005, the government commissioned a report on how to make Reykjavik an international financial center, like Luxembourg, Zurich,  or Hong Kong . Events in 2006 and 2007 challenged the Icelandic banks’ business model of heavy dependence on interbank funding in foreign currency. The krona and the stock market fell by a quarter in March 2006 when rating agency Fitch revised its sovereign outlook from stable to negative.* In response, the Iceland Chamber of Commerce commissioned a report with a prominent American economist as co-author that drew soothing conclusions about financial stability in Iceland.** The stock market resumed its climb. In March  2007, Fitch Ratings  downgraded the Icelandic sovereign from AA+, citing a current account deficit of 27 percent of GDP in 2006, with interest payments accounting for half that sum.*** (Fitch’s reference to ‘high standards of governance’ and ‘strong transparent institutions’ would not age well.) As noted above, distress was felt in international financial markets with the halting of redemptions at  the BNP Paribas  funds in August 2007. In the fall, the Iceland Chamber of Commerce commissioned a critical but again ultimately reassuring report on Icelandic banks with a prominent American economist as co-author.**** One of the Icelandic banks relied increasingly on retail funding in Britain and the Netherlands through an internet brand known  as Icesave , whose depositors came to rival in number the whole population of Iceland. At this stage, some foreign observers began to wonder whether the Icelandic banks had not grown too large for even a top-rated government to backstop. When Lehman Brothers failed in mid-September 2008, the Icelandic banks lost their remaining capacity to roll over their wholesale debt and could not pay the interest to foreign banks. Stock prices tanked, and first one and then within days the other two large banks defaulted. The loan losses of the Icelandic banks soared. The banks were put into receivership by the Icelandic authorities, who had no foreign exchange to pay to Icesave’s retail depositors in the UK and Netherlands. The UK authorities paid out to the UK retail depositors, and an ugly dispute ensued between Iceland and the UK and the Netherlands. In the end, the foreign assets of the Icelandic bank ended up covering the deposits, and the German banks and others holding the Icelandic bank’s bonds were left holding the bag. Iceland is famous for having prosecuted and jailed dozens of bankers, including CEOs, for a collective century of jail time. But as investigator Jared Bibler in his 2022 book  Iceland’s Secret: The Untold Story of the World’s Biggest Con  makes clear , the story is more ominous than this fact suggests. Bibler was lead investigator at Icelandic regulator the Financial Supervisory Authority whose probes into the banks’ manipulation of their own share prices culminated in bankers’ serving time in jail. But Bibler reports that the probes were only allowed to go so far before funding was cut off.
