       ‘The great merit of the Basle agreement [on swaps between central banks] ...is the availability of unlimited amounts of assistance through rediscounting in a period of crisis... Lines of credit must be unlimited...’ 1  So wrote Charles Kindleberger in 1967. Forty-one years later, unlimited credits between central banks made the transition from academic prescription to operational reality. This was  a Kindleberger moment . Thus, the international lender of last resort changed so much in the twenty-first century that it merits a separate chapter in this edition. In the Great Financial Crisis (GFC) of 2008, central bank swaps came to play a role almost without precedent, under circumstances without precedent, and in a size without precedent. The Fed’s motive is often said to be the financial stability goal of making good the lost dollar funding of non-US banks. But the Fed’s extension of dollar credit to non-US banks through its swaps with central  banks  served both to fix the transmission of the Fed’s monetary policy to key dollar borrowing rates and to counter the runs on non-US banks. Central  bank  swaps during the acute phase of the pandemic crisis in March 2020 confirmed their role as backstops to global dollar banking. Again, they succeeded in reversing a rise in the dollar London interbank rate (Libor) and relieving dollar funding shortages for non-US banks. In addition, the Fed in the spring of 2020 played a new role, well beyond  what Perry Mehrling  calls  the dealer of last resort . 2  The Fed’s role as buyer of  last resort  in the US bond market backstopped the global market for dollar bonds, including those issued outside the United States by non-US borrowers. Last resort buying extended from the money market to the capital market and ramified globally. The previous chapter identified the central  bank  swap network as an important innovation in the international lender of last resort. Central bank technicians meeting  at the Bank for International Settlements  (BIS) in Basel or talking over the telephone could agree to provide each other with their respective key currencies with speed, in size, and without policy conditions. By contrast, credit from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), with its almost universal membership, board meetings, and voting rules, takes time, is rule-bound in scale, and comes with policy conditions attached. These differences underlay the division of labor between central  bank  swaps and IMF credit, as described in the previous chapter. While swaps could speedily provide credit, they were to be repaid in months. Failing that, the borrower needed to turn to fully multilateral credit from the IMF to refinance the short-term swaps over the medium term. The use of central  bank  swaps in this century continues an evolution in their purposes since their origins in the 1960s. The swap network started out as one of the multiple devices to keep the fixed exchange rate system going. 3  When that system broke down with the beginning of generalized floating of major exchange rates in 1973, the swap network not only survived but expanded to support the management of major exchange rates through the 1970s. Then from 1982 through 1998, central  bank  swaps served at times as temporary bridges to IMF loans to developing (later called emerging market) economies that were experiencing difficulty in managing their external debt. In short, swaps morphed from major exchange rate management tool under first fixed then floating exchange rates to short-term bridge credit to IMF medium-term credit to Latin American and Asian debtors to banks. The central  bank  swaps of 2008 and 2020 made for a new chapter in this evolution. They did not serve the purpose of intervention in the foreign-exchange market. Nor did they bridge to IMF credit. Instead, along with other emergency measures of the Fed, the swaps kept dollar funding going to non-US banks. As sketched in the following section on global dollar banking, the dollar played an outsized global role and non-US banks predominated in dollar intermediation outside the United States. This had three key consequences for the Fed’s global last resort lending. First, it proved to be very large. In 2007–2008, the Fed advanced dollars to first a narrow and then a broad circle of central banks and ratcheted up the agreed amounts into the fall of 2008. In October, the Fed’s agreed to extend credit to five central banks without ex ante limits and the aggregate amounts advanced reached almost $600 billion. It took most of a trillion dollars to backstop just 5 percent of the dollar liabilities of non-US banks. In 2020, the amounts quickly reached almost $500 billion. This was  another Kindleberger moment . Second, such a scale broke the link between central  bank  swaps and potential IMF credit. Available IMF credit fell well short of the swaps. The Fed reassured the US Congress that the partner central bank took the risk of (secured) lending to the borrowing non-US banks, but in lending without limit the Fed’s trust in the partner central bank was complete. Nor was there in general a backstop at the national level. For instance, the maximum swap to the ECB well exceeded the foreign-exchange reserves of the ECB and the Eurosystem’s national central banks. Central  bank  swaps stood on their own feet as never before. Finally, the international last resort lending in 2008 overwhelmingly took the form of dollars, and thus it centered on the Fed. In the 1960s and 1970s, the Fed had been both lender and borrower in the reciprocal network of swaps; intra-European swaps were at times very sizeable from the 1960s until the introduction of the euro. 4  In 2008, the ECB  and Swiss National Bank  (SNB) also extended swaps to some European central banks to backstop, for example, respectively, Swedish banks’ funding of euro mortgages  in Latvia  and Polish banks’ funding of Swiss franc mortgages. But these regional operations were not large. Dollar predominance in private international banking made the Fed the global lender of last resort. Non-US Banks in Global Dollar Intermediation To understand the Fed as a global dollar lender of last resort, some perspective on the role of non-US banks in global dollar intermediation is useful. In the 50 years to 2008, the dollar’s domain had extended from the United States to Western Europe and then across the world. In the rest of the world, firms borrowed dollars from banks to finance trade, inventories, and their capital stock, governments borrowed to fund their debts and in some places, households even took on dollar-denominated home mortgages. On the eve of the GFC, nonbanks outside the United States had borrowed almost $4 trillion from banks (Fig.  13.1 , left panel). This was about double the sum of euro-denominated loans to nonbanks outside the euro area. As a currency for international borrowing, the dollar stood head and shoulders above its nearest rival. Banks headquartered outside the United States did the bulk of this dollar lending to the rest of the world. To fund these and other dollar assets, non-US banks had by 2008 accumulated $13 trillion of dollar liabilities, almost $10 trillion of which from nonbanks (Fig.  13.1 , right panel). 5  European and Japanese  banks  were the most prominent among the non-US banks. These banks actively managed these liabilities, depending on short-term funding to a considerable extent. Two area graphs depict non-US banks with three plots each for debt securities, bonds issued, and bank loans, and non-US banks by bank nationality with eight plots each. Fig. 13.1 On-balance sheet US dollar liabilities of non-banks outside of the United States and non-US banks. Amounts outstanding, in USD trillions. (1) Non-banks comprise non-bank financials, non-financial corporations, governments, households and international organisations. (2) Loans by LBS-reporting banks to non-bank borrowers, including non-bank financial entities, comprise cross-border plus local loans. (3) Non-US banks’ US dollar-denominated liabilities raised in any of the 47 BIS reporting countries (including the United States). Excludes intragroup positions but includes liabilities to other (unaffiliated) banks. From end-2015, includes positions reported by China and Russia ( Sources  Dealogic; Euroclear; Thomson Reuters; Xtrakter; BIS locational banking statistics; BIS calculations) Although the overwhelming share of the dollar liabilities of non-US banks was raised outside the United States, their biggest single source of dollar funding in 2008 was US dollar money market funds (MMFs). US dollar MMFs lent non-US banks at least $1.2 trillion, or at least an eighth of their nonbank funding. 6 Despite three decades of generally stable operation, MMFs were fragile by design. They operated without capital at the level of the fund, although losses could be covered by the fund sponsor. Despite the absence of capital, the US Securities and Exchange Commission allowed them to redeem their shares within limits as if they were worth $1 par. Calling these intermediaries shadow banks, as is often done, is at most half-right, however. These intermediaries to a considerable extent simply bundled together funding from firms and households to buy the IOUs of non-US banks. Shadow bank suggests an intermediary that competes with banks, not an intermediary that interacts symbiotically with certain banks. In addition, non-US banks in effect borrowed dollars at generally short maturities invisibly in the foreign-exchange swap market. For instance, a German bank could take a euro deposit and exchange it for dollars with a forward purchase of the euros against the dollars, in effect borrowing dollars against euro collateral. Then the bank could use the dollars to fund a dollar loan or a dollar bond holding. The amounts could only be roughly estimated, but banks had used such swaps to fund themselves in dollars on the order of a trillion dollars. 7 In the foreign-exchange swap market, big non-US banks mostly served as intermediaries, putting their balance sheets between those lending and borrowing dollars against other currencies. Among their most important counterparties  are insurance  companies and pension funds outside the United States who hold US dollar bonds and US equities on a hedged basis. For such institutional investors, the hedge would typically consist of a short-term forward sale of dollars against the home currency. These would be rolled at maturity as long as necessary. As a result, there tends to be a mismatch between the long-term dollar security that is being hedged and the hedge. In sum, by the twenty-first century the dollar had come to play an outsized role in international banking in a competitive market in which the winners were non-US banks. These depended on unsecured and secured short-term dollar funding markets and the ability to borrow dollars against other currencies. Both sources of dollars proved vulnerabilities. 
 The Fed as Global Dollar Backstop: The 1960s Precedents Shortly after non-US banks began to borrow and lend dollars outside the United States, funding strains emerged. Year-end window-dressing, financial turbulence, and war could all put up pressure on dollar funding and lead to unwelcome rises in offshore dollar yields. Recent archival work  with Catherine Schenk  has brought to light the use of dollar swaps to counter these offshore dollar funding strains in the 1960s. Thus, the international lender of last resort operations of 2007–2008 had important precedents 40 plus years before. 8  These formed an important part of the Basel-based central bank cooperaton that inspired Kindleberger to prescribe unlimited swaps. As described in the last chapter, in the mid-1960s, Charles Coombs, head of foreign-exchange operations at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, persuaded European central banks to enter into swap arrangements mostly as a means to defend the dollar’s fixed exchange rates. But right from the start, the New York Fed and the BIS agreed to a separate swap line designed to provide dollars to the BIS. The intention was precisely to manage strains in the fast-growing offshore dollar market. The operations that used this swap line lasted only a few years, but they anticipated the use of swaps in the present century, and also point to a more multilateral approach. From 1965 through 1968, dollar funding strains could appear with end-year window-dressing operations, as Swiss banks, in particular, sought temporarily to replace somewhat mysterious dollar assets with solid Swiss franc assets to be reported in their annual reports. In addition, surprising events like  the Six Day War  or the devaluation of the pound sterling later in 1967 could disturb dollar funding markets. In retrospect, these were mild strains, but they could put upward pressure on dollar rates in London and other offshore banking centers if left untreated. Higher dollar rates in London could in turn disturb the US domestic dollar market, sending signals regarding dollar interest rates at odds with Fed policy. To reduce such pressure, the New York Fed extended its operations abroad to match the spread of dollar markets across the Atlantic Ocean. The Fed advanced dollars to the BIS, and then money market dealers at this central bank condominium placed unsecured term deposits with mostly European banks offshore. The BIS played not just a coordinating role,  as Saleem Bahaj   and Ricardo Reis  describe it, but acted as a principal, taking the risk of lending on an unsecured basis to the commercial banks. 9  In some cases, the SNB was involved as well. In this manner, central banks sought to restrain the rise of dollar yields. The precedent for the twenty-first century lender of last resort is clear. In the mid-1960s, Federal Reserve credit flowed abroad to stabilize the funding of mostly non-US banks in the offshore dollar market. One difference from 2007 to 2008 was that a multilateral central banking organization served as intermediary between the Fed and the private banks that ultimately received the Fed credit. 
 Backstopping Global Dollar Banking, 2007–2008 To the vast offshore dollar intermediation described above, non-US banks in the 2000s added investments in US private mortgage-backed securities. They did so in manifold ways, as discussed in Chapter  2 . They borrowed dollars in the United States to fund ‘production line’ and ‘warehouse’ holdings in their US securities affiliates. They borrowed in the United States to fund holdings in their offshore offices. And they borrowed dollars offshore to fund holdings at offshore offices. 10  Non-US banks’ exposure to risky privately packaged mortgages drove the foreign-held share of such securities to over 40 percent. As US house prices peaked in 2006 and fell in 2007, the US real estate mania passed into distress. Bankers uneasily wondered at each others’ holdings of, and prospective losses on, fiendishly complicated securities backed by US mortgages. Central bank reserve managers began in the latter half of 2007 to withdraw some of the $600 billion in liquid dollar reserves held in offshore deposits at what had been the best-rated banks. These credit-conscious reserve managers responded to news indicating that such seemingly strong non-US banks had sizeable exposures to highly leveraged US mortgages. In the latter half of 2007, they reduced deposits with Swiss banks and proceeded subsequently to reduce deposits with most other European banks. 11  It was a slow run, by the standards of the later run after the Lehman failure on MMFs, and in turn their run on non-US banks. Unease turned into distress on 9 August  2007. BNP Paribas  chillingly announced the suspension of redemptions from funds holding US private mortgage-backed securities that were hedged into euro, citing ‘the complete evaporation of liquidity in certain market segments of the US securitization market [that] has made it impossible to value certain assets fairly, regardless of their quality or credit rating.’ 12  The ECB quickly extended €95 billion to banks in an attempt to keep the interbank market working. The Fed cut its discount rate on bilateral loans, but banks avoided one by one approaches to the discount window, lest they bear the stigma of needing such central bank credit. Recall that European banks had a large structural need to borrow dollars, and did much at short maturity relative to the maturity of their dollar assets. If they, like  the BNP Paribas  funds, were holding unknown amounts of private mortgage-backed securities that were impossible to value, how could they roll over trillions of dollars in short-term dollar funding? The Fed ultimately supported the dollar funding of non-US banks in three ways. First, the Fed set up a stigma-free version of its discount window, on which non-US banks drew heavily, and supplemented it with parallel dollar provision in Europe funded with swaps with the ECB and SNB. Second, the Fed used its emergency powers to stop the run on MMFs that heavily funded non-US banks and to  support commercial paper . And, third, breaking the link to the discount window, the Fed swapped dollars with its partner central banks in ultimately unlimited amounts so that they could provide dollars offshore to non-US banks. In September 2007, as the Fed considered proposals to turn its discount window into a broad auction facility (similar to the usual ECB facilities), discussions began on a central  bank  swap between the Fed and the ECB. As later recalled by Fed and Treasury officials, ‘The ECB initially sought to strike a posture that it was merely supporting the Fed’s efforts to counter US-centric and dollar-centric stresses, rather than embracing its role as the Fed’s full partner in fighting a crisis that was centered in the United States but that had truly global dimensions.’ 13  If the Fed were to auction off 28-day discount window credit (in  the Term Auction Facility  or TAF), then the ECB would be happy to join the operation, in effect serving as the 13th Federal Reserve Bank, in the phrase of Francesco Papadia, then head of ECB operations. 14  In December 2007, the Fed and ECB agreed on a swap that would allow the latter, in coordination with the TAF operations, to lend up to $20 billion to banks in Europe against euro-denominated collateral. The Fed and the SNB agreed $4 billion. Until the failure of Lehman Brothers in September 2008, non-US banks obtained more dollars from the TAF, using their US assets as collateral for Fed credit at the discount window, than from the ECB and SNB, using European collateral. TAF borrowers did not know  that Bloomberg   and Fox News  would eventually succeed in 2011 in a freedom of information request for full disclosure of the TAF transactions: names, amounts, dates, etc. As a result, we know that, on the eve of the Lehman failure, the Fed had extended most of the TAF credit of $150 billion to foreign banks’ US operations, 15  while the ECB swap line had risen to $55 billion and the SNB to $6 billion. 16  The discount window at the Second District Federal Reserve Bank of New York was doing the heavy lifting until September 2008. Lehman’s failure set off a run on non-US banks’ most important single dollar source, MMFs. One of the oldest MMFs,  the Reserve Primary Fund , ‘broke the buck,’ showing a net asset value below a dollar as it accounted for losses on  Lehman commercial paper . The fund had no deep-pocketed sponsor that could make up the credit loss, as had been done before and after under these circumstances. Institutional investors redeemed shares in other MMFs holding bank and corporate paper. Within days, non-US banks had lost at least $175 billion of MMF funding, despite a rapid succession of policy measures. 17  This was a fast run. The resulting ‘dollar shortage’ implied a rise in dollar interest rates payable in the rest of the world, in both cash markets and the foreign exchange forward market. Non-US banks bid up Libor, the London benchmark short-term dollar interest rate for (increasingly scarce) unsecured funding. The rate payable by those borrowing dollars against the euro and other currencies soared in the foreign-exchange swap market. These borrowed dollars became the marginal financing for dollar assets held by banks. And as the premium on dollars rose, it boosted the cost of hedging trillions of dollars of dollar bonds and US equities held by institutional investors outside the United States. Punishing dollar rates for the rest of the world thus not only threatened tighter financing terms for firms and governments that had borrowed $4 trillion from banks. Such rates also risked banks’ and institutional investors’ liquidating dollar assets  in fire sales . The US authorities took emergency measures to stop the run on MMFs, and thereby stop their run on non-US banks. The policies included a Treasury guarantee the par value of MMFs, and Fed facilities to buy and  underwrite commercial paper , both of which would reduce the rollover risk of holding such paper. In the first instance, these were domestic lender of last resort operations that sought to stabilize MMFs. But these policy interventions to support MMFs and the commercial paper market served at one remove as international lender of last resort operations: ending runs on the riskier MMFs ended their liquidation of claims on non-US banks. After the Lehman failure, central banks expanded their swap lines to replace the private dollar funding that non-US banks were losing. Initially, the swap line with the ECB was doubled to $110 billion, and that to the SNB was quadrupled. The Fed agreed new lines for the Bank of Japan, Bank of England, and  the Bank of Canada  totaling $110 billion. On 29 September, central banks agreed to at least double all these swap lines. On 13 October central banks announced fatefully that ‘sizes of the reciprocal currency arrangements (swap lines) between the Federal Reserve and the BoE, the ECB, and the SNB [and the Bank of  Japan  on the following day] will be increased to accommodate whatever quantity of US dollar funding is demanded [at fixed rates].’  As Jaime Caruana , General Manager of the BIS noted later, ‘the extension of such swaps in unlimited amounts represents a turn in central bank cooperation that the founders of the BIS [in the 1920s] would have found unimaginable.’ 18 Non-US banks revealed a preference for the Fed’s international lending of last resort through swaps over drawing on the domestic lending of last resort through the discount window. That is, as the swaps became unlimited, non-US banks responded by reducing their takings from the TAF even as they ramped up their takings from the swaps. 19  To continue with the metaphor, credit from the 13th Federal  Reserve Bank  displaced that from the 2nd District Bank in New York. Non-US banks thereby retained scarce US collateral that would allow them to draw on the Fed’s discount window late in the day. The credit risk of lending to non-US banks shifted from the Federal Reserve to the ECB and other central banks. At the peak, the Fed had swapped almost $600 billion, mostly to the ECB, the SNB, the Bank of England, and a few other central banks. These in turn distributed the funds to banks that could offer collateral that these central banks found satisfactory. The Fed’s open-handedness worked to lower the short-term dollar rates that mattered most. After Lehman’s collapse, expected overnight rates had trended unevenly down (lower line in the upper panel of Fig.  13.2 ), and the Fed lowered its target for the federal funds rate by 50 basis points at its October 8 meeting. But the Fed easing was not making itself felt in rates paid by US corporations on their bank loans or by US households on their adjustable-rate mortgages. Libor doubled from less than 3 percent before Lehman’s failure. The spread between the Fed’s expected overnight rates and Libor hit 4 percent (shaded area in the lower panel of Fig.  13.2 ). After 13 October, without ex ante limits on the swaps to the key central banks, this spread fell by half within weeks. 20  The compression of 3-month Libor might have happened even faster had the central banks offered unlimited dollar funding at this maturity in October, as they later did in November 2008. The line and area graphs depict the dollar from August to December 2008, with two curves: swap and offered rates in the line graph and Libro O I S in the area graph. Fig. 13.2 Central bank swaps lower dollar Libor, late 2008 ( Source  Refinitiv Datastream; Federal Reserve; author’s calculations) Likewise, the rate premium for borrowing dollars against foreign-exchange collateral narrowed in response to the expansion of the swap lines. 21  That is, the rate at which non-US banks could borrow dollars against the euro, yen, and other currencies fell back toward outright dollar borrowing rates like Libor or repurchase rates. Institutional investors outside the United States were able to roll over hedges of US securities holdings, instead of engaging  in fire sales . Unlimited swaps effectively backstopped both the offshore deposit market and the forward foreign-exchange market. 22 Often the motivation for the swaps is ascribed to the Fed’s goal of financial stability, 23   and Daniel McDowell   in his book,  Brother Can You Spare a Billion  stands out in recognizing their key role in fixing the Fed’s monetary transmission to the US economy. 24  Libor priced not only trillions of dollars of derivative contracts but also, it bears repeating, US corporate loans and US adjustable-rate mortgages. While the October 2008 FOMC meeting dwelled on the difficulty of controlling the opening federal funds rate in New York given upward pressure offshore, the transmission of the Fed’s policy rate to the domestic real economy required a lower 3-month Libor, not just hitting the overnight fed funds target. 25  Non-US banks dominated the panel of banks that reported Libor at 11 a.m., 6 a.m. New York time. So the New York Fed needed to ease term funding conditions by dawn for non-US banks offshore, and the swaps put dollars into the hands of central bankers in Frankfurt, London, and Zurich to do just that job. Ultimately, the Fed reconciled its domestic Congressional mandate with its providing a backstop to offshore dollar banking. It extended hundreds of billions of dollars in central bank credit to stabilize trillions of offshore dollars for which non-US banks were liable. It did so not only to achieve the global public good of financial stability but also to assure the transmission of its monetary policy to US households and businesses. 
 The Fed Backstops Global Dollar Banking and Bonds, 2020 When a very different funding crisis next struck amid pandemia in March 2020, the Fed not only returned to its playbook but also extended it very significantly. Again, it sought to stop the run on MMFs. Again, it activated the swap lines with major central banks and extended them more broadly. But this time, severe disruption of the dollar bond market led the Fed to become a buyer of  last resort  in the bond market. Without targeting foreign involvement in the dollar bond market per se, domestic Fed bond purchases accommodated sales of Treasury securities by foreign central banks and helped to stabilize prices of trillions of dollars of foreign-issued dollar bonds. Indirectly, the Fed backstopped the global dollar bond market. When in March 2020 market participants began to understand the challenge of  the Covid  pandemic, they responded in a dash for cash. Firms worried that revenues would crash to zero, leaving cash flows deeply negative. The ‘cash’ resources of the corporate treasury, often invested more for yield than immediate availability, suddenly needed to be really liquid. And firms drew down credit lines with banks to bulk up on bank deposits. Banks did not suffer runs, as in 2008, but they prepared for large cash calls on committed lines of credit. As in 2008, the riskier MMFs suffered runs. Investing in bank and corporate IOUs, ‘prime’ MMFs experienced redemptions of $125 billion in March 2020, 11 percent of their assets. 26  This was a smaller liquidation than in 2008, when this segment of MMFs was larger. This time none broke the buck or impeded liquidations. Still, as MMFs paid out to redeem shares, remaining shareholders worried that dwindling liquid assets would trigger ‘gates’—constraints on redemptions mandated by regulators after 2008. A reform to deal with liquidity strains on MMFs turned out to accelerate runs. 27 As in 2008, the run on MMFs had knock-on effects on other markets. It threatened to close  the commercial paper  market, a key source of short-term financing for firms. And, as in 2008, the run on MMFs left non-US banks scrambling for dollars. Onshore and offshore MMF funding of non-US banks dropped by $200 billion in February–March 2020. 28 The dash for cash did not just disrupt money markets, however. It also led to the selling of US dollar bonds. This selling not only destabilized the global benchmark bond  market—the US Treasury bond  market—but also the main funding source for US corporations. As background, US corporate  bonds  outstanding had grown very considerably since the GFC, in part as an  intended  consequence of the Fed’s repeated rounds of bond buying. The Fed encouraged US corporations to issue bonds by buying  Treasury  and  agency  mortgage securities, reducing the so-called term premium demanded for locking in funding for years at a fixed rate. As an  unintended  consequence of the same Fed bond buying, firms, and governments outside the United States had also issued dollar bonds in size. As a result, the rest of the world’s borrowing in the dollar had shifted over the previous decade away from bank loans to dollar bonds (Fig.  13.1 , left panel). In March 2020, heavy selling of bonds came from three sides. First, hedge funds dumped US Treasuries. Highly leveraged so-called relative value funds held relatively cheap Treasury  bonds  (financed in the repo market) against short positions in Treasury bond futures. The normally modest spread between these two—certain cash bonds could be periodically delivered into maturing bond futures, linking their prices—widened amid rising volatility, increasing margins, and deteriorating liquidity. This wrong way move cost the highly leveraged funds dearly. Losses in turn forced them to deleverage by selling Treasuries in the hundreds of billions of dollars in March. Other hedge fund strategies magnified the moves. 29  Lots of leverage among holders could make even a safe asset risky. The data are partial, but something well over $200 billion in hedge fund selling is a reasonable estimate. 30 Second, foreign central banks also dumped Treasuries. Recalling the pressure on their dollar borrowing banks and firms in 2008, and in many cases intervening in the foreign-exchange market to support their currencies by selling dollars, they sought to turn Treasury holdings into immediately useful bank deposits. Treasury data show $244 billion  in US Treasury bond  sales, or 3.3 percent of holdings, by foreign officials in March–May 2020. 31 Third, responding to and magnifying these sales, households staged the largest and sharpest liquidation of bond mutual funds in memory, and the run forced fund managers to sell bonds in the market. Since the GFC, low interest rates had encouraged US households to reach for yield by buying bond mutual funds. US bond fund holdings as a share of the corporate bond market rose from less than a tenth to almost a fifth. Facing the uncertainties of pandemic and turmoil in the bond market, households liquidated an unprecedented 5.6 percent of bond fund assets in March. 32  One interpretation is that households originally viewed this investment as only slightly riskier than a bank deposit but in March 2020 suddenly viewed it as risky. 33  Another interpretation is that given the hedge fund and foreign selling of Treasury  bonds  and their resultant yield spike in early to mid-March 2020, bond fund holders redeemed about what one would expect in response to recently experienced price declines. 34  In any case, bond fund managers had little choice but to pass on the selling pressure to the bond market. The easiest bonds to sell were US Treasuries, and funds sold $260 billion in the first quarter of 2020. 35 Stepping back, then, the Fed faced big runs on money and bond mutual funds and widespread dumping of US bonds. Holders of the riskier MMFs sought out, pulling dollars out of non-US banks. The Fed dealt with this as it had in 2008. But what to do in the face of large selling of US Treasury securities and an incipient run on bond mutual funds? This required a new playbook. At risk was the main source of funding for US corporations—and for nonbank dollar borrowers outside the United States as well. The Fed responded with a combination of old and new policies. It dealt with the disruption of the money markets along the lines of its response in 2008 but innovated in its response to the disruption of the bond markets. To calm bond markets, the Fed became the buyer of  last resort  in a manner that had profound international implications. To underscore: the Fed did not target foreign holdings of US bonds or foreign-issued dollar bonds in particular. Nevertheless, the effect of the Fed bond buying on foreign holdings of US bonds and foreign-issued dollar bonds amounts to an extension of its international lender of last resort operations. The Fed quickly consulted its playbook from 2008 to stabilize MMFs and thereby to stabilize their funding of non-US banks. The Fed rolled out facilities to inject its credit into  the commercial paper  market as a buyer of  last resort . 36  In order to increase the confidence of MMF investors, on March 17 it revived a program to underwrite new issues  of commercial paper , reassuring investors that maturing paper could be rolled over. On March 18, it revived a 2008 facility to allow the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston in effect to buy outstanding commercial paper (not just asset-backed commercial paper as in 2008) held by MMFs (technically lending on a non-recourse basis to banks to buy the paper). To enable non-US banks to access dollars and thereby replace the loss of funding from MMFs, the Fed reactivated the swap lines. In 2007–2008, the Fed had taken a year to widen access to larger amounts for more central banks, for longer maturities, and in more frequent operations. Playbook in hand, the Fed took these steps in days in March 2020. Once again, as non-US banks scrambled for dollars, Libor began lifting off from the Fed’s policy interest rate. Even as the Fed lowered its federal fund policy rate, as reflected in the expected overnight  rate (the overnight index swap  or OIS, plotted as the lower line in the upper panel of Fig.  13.3) , the key 3-month Libor rate began to rise on 12 March. A line and area graph indicates the dollar versus February to May 2020 containing daily ops start, 5 core abs, 9 central banks added in a line graph, and Libro O I S spread in the area graph. Fig. 13.3 Central bank swaps lower dollar Libor, early 2020 ( Source  Refinitiv Datastream; Federal Reserve; author’s calculations) Swiftly, the Fed acted to keep the transmission of its interest rate policy to the real economy from breaking down by extending its credit offshore to bring down Libor. The very next day, the Fed eased its interest rate on central bank swaps from OIS+50 basis points to OIS+25 basis points for five core central banks with standing swaps; it also offered 84-day swaps. Libor fell but then began to rise again and the Fed extended the swaps to the other nine central banks on March 19 and started daily operations. The start of daily swap operations on March 23 marked the local maximum of Libor, which fell to within 25 basis points of OIS by early May. With these swift moves, Fed credit extended to central banks through swaps rose much more sharply in 2020 than in 2008 but peaked at a lower level at less than $500 billion. The political reaction to the use of swaps in 2020 confounded widespread fears that de facto the Fed faced a higher political hurdle to mobilize the swaps. In 2008 and after, the Fed fielded sharp questions from Congress regarding the central  bank  swaps. 37  In the end, the new banking legislation known as the Dodd-Frank Act did nothing to restrict the legal ability of the Fed to extend its credit to other central banks through swaps. This absence of constraint stood in contrast to new constraints on the Fed’s use of its emergency lending powers, which proscribed deals for individual firms (as with Bear Stearns in March 2008 and AIG in September 2008) and required Treasury assent. Still, there was a practical political question about the use of swaps. In the event, central  bank  swaps caused little controversy in 2020. The balance of the swaps shifted from Europe in 2008 to Asia, that  is, Japan , in 2020. In 2008, the ECB borrowed about half of the dollars advance by the Fed; in 2020, the Bank of Japan did. This partly reflected the retrenchment of European banks after the traumas, near-death experiences, and nationalizations of 2008. It also reflected the fact that the international banking footprint of Japanese banks 38  had expanded since the GFC. 39  Strong growth in holdings of dollar bonds on a hedged basis by  Asian insurance  companies also boosted demand to borrow dollars in the foreign-exchange market. 40 In response to Treasury bond selling and the spike in Treasury rates, the Fed entered the market as a determined, rapid, and heavy buyer. The operating instruction to the open-market desk at the New York Fed charged it with buying Treasury and agency securities ‘in the amounts needed’ to restore the proper functioning of the market. 41  In the three weeks between 11 March and 2 April, the Fed bought no less than $900 billion of Treasury and agency securities. 42  Thus, Fed more than offset the domestic and foreign official selling of US Treasuries of as much as $800 billion over a longer period. From the standpoint of the foreign official holders of US Treasury securities, the Fed purchases allowed them to turn securities with wildly fluctuating prices set in suddenly and surprisingly illiquid markets into bank deposits or secured placements with the New York Fed (repos). Watching central banks selling US Treasuries, only to see them sit on much of the cash at the New York Fed, led the Fed at the end of March to offer overnight advances to central banks using US Treasuries as collateral at a rate above private repo rates. This little-used facility, dubbed  the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities (FIMA) Repo Facility , is discussed below. Dislocations were evident in the corporate bond market as well and the Fed responded speedily. As mutual funds sold corporate  bonds , these went to big discounts to levels implied by credit derivatives. Such market dynamics threatened to cut off US firms’ major source of financing of investment and hiring, and even to cause defaults if maturing bonds could not be refinanced. On March 17, the Fed announced that it would use its emergency powers to lend to its primary dealers, i.e., its bond market counterparties, as it had in 2008. This gave them an assurance of funding that would allow them to make markets and arbitrage cash and derivatives markets. On March 20 the Fed extended the first loans to the primary dealers using these emergency powers. The primary dealers offered corporate bonds as collateral for the Fed advances, suggesting that the Fed credit was getting through the dealers to support the corporate bond market. The Fed then took an unprecedented step as a corporate bond buyer of  last resort . On March 23, it announced  that it would buy investment grade US corporate  bonds . The principle of the Fed buying  corporate commercial paper  at money market tenors had been set in 2008 and reinforced earlier in the month with the revival of the commercial paper buying program. What was unprecedented was the Fed going beyond the money market, the usual focus of its operations. The Fed was backstopping the longer-maturity private bonds on which US firms rely most for market funding. The Fed’s terms for the corporate bond purchases showed a sensitivity to the political hazard of being seen to help firms without a direct stake in the US economy. To be purchased, a bond issuer could be foreign-owned but had to be incorporated in the United States, have significant US operations and a majority of its employees based in the United States. 43  This targeted intention, however, did not preclude that the program would indirectly lift the prices of dollar bonds issued by foreign firms that did not meet these criteria. More surprising was the announcement on April 9 that the Fed would buy junk bonds, the low-rated bonds of more leveraged and more risky firms. After all, the Fed as bank regulator had been flagging for years to banks the risks of lending to firms that private equity firms were loading up with debt, both bank loans and junk bonds. Indeed, ultimately the Fed bought mutual finds designed to hold the whole gamut of junk bonds, so the Fed bought some bonds that had been issued by firms that the Fed had cautioned banks not to lend to. 44 In any case, one can imagine that the corporate bond purchases could affect non-Treasury dollar bond prices in one of two ways. The Fed buying could be a thumb on the scale of just those bonds purchased. There was certainly evidence for such: the Fed’s announcement highlighted its intention to lower yields on short- to medium-term bonds, and their yields fell more markedly, for instance. Alternatively, the effect of the Fed buying could diffuse from those bonds purchased across the spectrum of dollar bonds embodying credit risk. This diffusion could work through portfolio substitution by investors, as they sold into the prospective Fed bid for US corporate  bonds  and bought cheaper bonds not targeted by the Fed. The prices  of the biggest ETFs  for investment grade US corporate  bonds , junk US corporate bonds, and emerging market dollar bonds broadly support the second view. Prices of the ETFs for investment grade bonds (LQD) and emerging market bonds (EMB) had both bottomed between the Fed announcement of its lending to the primary dealers late on March 17 and its doing so on March 20 (Fig.  13.4 ). This timing points to funding liquidity rather than credit concerns, reinforcing the impression conveyed by the gap between US corporate cash bond prices and those of the corresponding credit derivatives. When the Fed announced that it would buy investment grade bonds, the  price of their ETF  rose for three days. With a one-day lag, both the junk bond and emerging market ETF prices rose for three days as well. When the Fed announced that it would buy junk bonds on April 9 and upped its overall maximum of corporate bond purchases, the prices of all three ETFs jumped the same day. By mid-June 2020, the prices  of all three ETFs  had recovered substantially. Though the Fed bought corporate  bonds  and did not buy any of the emerging market dollar bonds, their price performance did not much differ. The effect of the Fed's purchase of US corporate bonds seemed to diffuse widely. A line graph represents the values ranging from 70 through 105 versus March to June 2020 with four curves, as well as fed to buy U S corporate, and junk bonds, fed to lend to primary dealers. Fig. 13.4 Emerging market dollar bonds rise as the Federal Reserve buys US corporate bonds ( Source  Refinitiv Datastream; Federal Reserve; author’s calculations) Flows into bond funds also point to the conclusion that the Fed’s promise to purchase US corporate  bonds  turned around flows into global bond funds. Outflows from global bond funds seemed to respond more quickly to the Fed announcement than did outflows from US investment grade bonds (Fig.  13.5 ). But broadly flows into the bonds that the Fed never bought tracked those of the ones that it did buy. With the flows, as with the prices, the effect of the Fed announcement seemed to diffuse beyond US corporate bonds to dollar bonds from issuers in the rest of the world. A line graph depicts the billions of dollars per week with three curves U S investment grade bond flow, U S junk bond flow, and global bond flow with a peak value is 5. Fig. 13.5 Global bond flows recover as the Federal Reserve buys US corporate bonds ( Source  Refinitiv Datastream; Federal Reserve; Investment Company Institute; author’s calculations) In sum, in March 2020, the combination of the Fed’s lending of last resort to securities dealers and its buying of last resort of US corporate  bonds  had an unintended consequence. Not only US corporate  bonds  but also global dollar bonds bottomed in price between the announcement of the primary dealer lending and the first loans. One can interpret this observation as suggesting that Fed credit allowed the primary dealers to make markets in all sorts of dollar bonds embodying credit risk, both domestic and foreign. And the subsequently similar price movements in the US corporate and global bonds point to investors’ evident treatment of domestic and foreign dollar bonds as close substitutes in their credit portfolios. Lending to bond dealers and buying bonds domestically, the Fed halted an incipient run on funds holding dollar bonds issued by non-US obligors. Stopping the outflows from global bond funds in turn  prevented fire sales  of dollar bonds issued by borrowers outside the United States. In effect, if not in intention, the Fed backstopped the global dollar bond market. 
 The Who’s Who of Swap Lines In extending swap lines, the Fed has drawn three lines. The Fed has established standing swap lines with Canada, the Bank of England, the ECB, the Bank of Japan, and the SNB. These lines have no ex ante fixed limits in terms of the number of dollars extended. Drawing a second line, the Fed has established temporary lines with five advanced economies—the main Nordic countries (Denmark, Norway, and  Sweden), Australia  and New Zealand—and four  emerging economies—Brazil , Mexico, Singapore, and South Korea. The Fed has drawn a third line that includes any central bank that holds US Treasuries in custody at the New York Fed. Under the FIMA repo facility, any central bank with US Treasury securities held in custody at the New York Fed can raise overnight funding from the Fed using those securities as collateral. 45  Little used, the facility became a standing one in July 2021. It complements the New York Fed’s reverse repo pool, which allows central banks to invest overnight cash. As might be readily imagined, such line drawing has led to a great deal of discussion among all kinds of observers. One line of inquiry has been the reverse engineering of the Fed’s choices: trade relations, banking exposure, politico-military relations, and UN voting alignment, among other factors, have attracted attention. 46 An aspect of the who’s who that has not received the attention that it deserves is the key currency aspect, that is, the coverage by the Fed’s central  bank  swaps of private foreign-exchange market swaps against dollars. Recall from the description of non-US banks in dollar intermediation above that non-US banks borrow and lend dollars not only on balance sheet but also off-balance sheet against foreign currencies. In choosing its central bank counterparties, the Fed’s focus on key currencies has resulted in quite high coverage of the largest segment, namely foreign-exchange swaps, of the huge global foreign-exchange market. The central bank survey of foreign-exchange markets in April 2019 found daily total turnover of $6.5 trillion, of which swaps accounted for about half. More than 90 percent of the swaps had the dollar on one side of the transaction. Thus, every working day in April 2019, dollars were borrowed and lent against other currencies to the extent of almost $3 trillion. The currencies of the five central banks with standing swap lines with the Fed account for two-thirds of the daily dollar lending through swaps. The currencies of the other nine central banks chosen by the Fed account for another 16 percent of dollar swap transactions (Fig.  13.6 ). Overall, the coverage of the currencies of the Fed’s 14 partner central banks in foreign-exchange swaps against dollars is five-sixths. A pie chart depicts the four breakdowns, with maximum E U R, J P Y, C H F, C A D, minimum B R L, K R W, M X P, S G D, and remaining portions A U D, D K K, N O K, N Z D, and S E K. Fig. 13.6 The Federal Reserve’s central bank swap lines cover most foreign exchange market swaps. Share of currencies by central bank swap line status in $2.9 trillion of daily dollar swaps, April 2019 Thus, the standing swap lines draw what may seem to be a narrow circle around five central banks, but actually draw a broad circle in terms of the currencies against which dollars are borrowed in the foreign-exchange market. 47  Adding the temporary swap lines with another nine central banks makes for a very broad circle, judged by dollar borrowing against foreign exchange. This perspective leads to a new interpretation of the finding of studies that the central  bank  swaps, especially in unlimited size, succeeded in lowering dollar borrowing costs in the respective currencies compared to such costs in ‘untreated’ currencies. 48  If the problem is the global tightening of dollar rates, then the central  bank  swaps involving the key currencies can solve most of the problem. And the temporary swaps take the share of the problem solved up to five-sixths. Even this way of looking at the swaps is liable to understate their effectiveness. In 2020, when the ECB obtained dollars from the Fed and lent them out to banks in the euro area, much of the proceeds were indeed lent in the foreign-exchange market in swaps against euros. 49  But by no means all were so lent. 50 A particularly suggestive case was  the Swedish kroner  in March 2020. The premium on dollars lent against the Swedish kroner in the foreign-exchange market tracked that against the euro very closely. 51  In particular, the two narrowed in lockstep as the ECB drew on its Fed swap to make dollars available to banks in the euro area. This was days before the Riksbank had agreed a swap with the New York Fed and weeks before the Riksbank’s first dollar-providing operation. A Riksbank study concluded: ‘The foreign-exchange swap market in Europe, including Sweden, started to function better particularly once the ECB commenced its extensive dollar auctions.’ 52 How could this have happened? Among the dollar takers from the ECB could have been affiliates of Swedish banks in Frankfurt that used the dollars to lend  against Swedish kroner  in the swap market. Or a French bank might have seen more return in lending dollars obtained from the ECB against kroner than against the euro. In either case, a  Swedish insurance  company could have been the counterparty, rolling over its dollar borrowing through a swap against kroner in order to maintain a currency hedge on a US dollar bond holding. As the Fed provided dollars to the ECB, the cost of the dollar hedge paid by the Swedish insurer normalized. In general, what starts as an official swap of dollars against euros can ultimately fund a private swap of dollars against any currency. Dollar borrowing costs in the currency of the central bank providing the dollars might be the first to show the effect. But the effect of the Fed’s swaps with the selected central banks can diffuse and lower dollar borrowing costs against other currencies. Such diffusion may have worked better in 2020 than it did in 2008, when big banks were not well capitalized, and possible credit losses inhibited transactions. One should not be surprised that the effect of the selected central  bank  swaps can spread widely across currencies in the foreign-exchange market. 53 The upshot is that it may not make such a large difference as is generally supposed that the Fed offers most of its swaps to a handful of central banks, given the large share of their respective key currencies in the foreign-exchange market. Note the family resemblance between two suggestions in this chapter: that the seeming narrowness of the choice of central bank counterparties for swaps and the Fed’s restriction of last resort bond buying to US bonds may not have mattered as much as one might suppose. The Fed decides with which central banks to establish swap lines and which dollar bonds to buy, but market participants decide how broadly the effect of Fed credit spreads. Despite the lines that the Fed drew, it managed in 2020 to ameliorate offshore dollar borrowing costs broadly, in banking and bond markets alike. In 2008 and 2020, the Fed proved willing and able to follow Kindleberger’s rule for the international lender of last resort, swapping dollars without limit to central banks to onlend to non-US banks. In doing so, the Fed not only provided the global public good of financial stability but also ensured the effectiveness of its domestic monetary policy. In 2020, the Fed’s unprecedented domestic bond market operations stabilized the global dollar bond market. Chapter  15  returns to these findings to pose two questions. How might central  bank  swaps support cooperative central bank operations in the global dollar bond market? And could politics constrain the Fed’s provision of the public good of international last resort lending? ‘Overfunding’ by the Treasury: a complement to the lender of last resort? A modern bank run is from bank deposits into Treasury bills as the ultimate safe asset, rather than into cash or gold. This was the case in 2008, but not in 2020, when the liquidity of bank deposits was more in demand than the safety of Treasury bills. In the case of a bank run into Treasury bills, it makes sense to complement the lender of last resort with the borrower of last resort in precisely the instrument in demand. If Congressional constraints on the Treasury’s debt permit, Treasury ‘overfunding’ in a crisis marked by a flight to quality can be stabilizing. In 2008, two groups of investors ran from banks into Treasury paper. Foreign central banks, starting already in 2007, reduced their placements with commercial banks. In the third and fourth quarters of 2008, foreign central banks added almost $500 billion to their holdings of Treasury bills, while private foreign investors added half that sum.* After Lehman’s failure, holders of ‘prime’ US money market funds, invested in the dollar debts of non-US banks, switched to government funds that invest in US Treasury bills. An important but overlooked complement of the international lender of last resort operation by the US authorities in 2008 was the US Treasury supply of bills in excess of its borrowing needs, reaching an amount near $600 billion. The rationale of the Treasury’s so-called supplementary financing account was to help the Fed to keep its target federal funds rate well above zero interest rates at a time when the Fed’s credit operations were otherwise creating excess reserves for banks. (Technically, the Treasury sold bills and deposited the proceeds at the Fed; the Fed did not yet have Congressional authority to pay interest on excess reserves.) This cooperation between the Fed and Treasury ultimately proved short-lived as the Treasury approached a debt limit. But whatever the intention and whatever the constraints, it was a useful tool of crisis management in late 2008 to supply the world’s safest of safe assets in an elastic manner—not determined by the size of the fiscal deficit or normal debt management policy. * Robert McCauley  and Patrick McGuire , ‘Dollar Appreciation in 2008: Safe Haven, Carry Trades, Dollar Shortage and Overhedging,'  BIS Quarterly Review , December 2009, pp. 85–93.          14. Bitcoin: Worse Than a Ponzi 
       
       
         
           Robert Z. Aliber 1     ,  
           Charles P. Kindleberger 2  and  
           
             Robert N. McCauley
