       The novel mania of the first decades of the twenty-first century  was an investment in cryptocurrencies  or cryptocoins. These are encoded units of value that are transferred over the internet from one holder to another on a decentralized ledger. In principle, if not in practice, no trusted institution oversees the transfers. And the electronic unit of value is not an IOU—it is a virtual asset but no one’s liability. Cryptocurrencies have proliferated as speculative assets, attracted many  investors, and produced billionaires. Cryptocurrencies  of various kinds have risen in number from one in 2009 to over 10,000 today. Despite the original promise of bilateral transfers, crypto holders can trade on hundreds of mostly unregulated exchanges. About 16 percent of Americans had invested in or traded cryptocurrencies by late 2021, including 43 percent of young men between 18 and 29 years of age. 1  The aggregate value of crypto reached about $3 trillion in November 2021, alongside the peak in US technology shares. In early 2018, Forbes listed 10 crypto billionaires, many of whom were founders of coins and exchanges. By March 2022, Forbes counted 19 crypto billionaires, including  Changpeng Zhao , founder of the leading trading  platform Binance . 2 For the leading cryptocurrency , bitcoin , there are three main sources of supply and demand: so-called miners, early investors, and late investors. First, a miner wins new 6.25 bitcoins by using brute computational force to discover a code, using the code to bundle thousands of pending transfers into a block, and attaching the new block to the extant chain of blocks  (hence ‘blockchain ’). 3  Second are the early investors in bitcoin , including some miners who do not sell their bitcoin rewards. The miners and early investors traded the bitcoin higher among each other, alongside some criminals who prized the promise of anonymous transfers. Third are the late  investors. Bitcoin  throws off no cash flow and no one stands to redeem it. Ultimately, early investors realize a gain only with a sale to late investors. Stepping back, one sees that investors became willing to pay a large sum for entries on no one’s spreadsheet. This happened even  as bitcoin’s  original rationale as anonymous means of value transfer gave way to a speculative and highly volatile store of value. As store of value, crypto turned out not to provide any hedge against inflation as crypto prices fell sharply in the first half of 2022 amid heightened inflation. Many prominent economists have expressed skepticism regarding bitcoin and its ilk. Nevertheless, they have struggled to analyze it, often labeling it a Ponzi scheme. Given the remarkable trajectory of crypto, it merits a more careful characterization. The verdict here is that Ponzi scheme does not fit. Ponzi schemes like the original and Madoff’s are subject to runs, but crypto is not. Investors cannot collectively call time on crypto. At heart crypto is less Ponzi  than pump and dump , as described in the box below. Crypto ends not in a run, but in a price crash, a ‘go to zero’ as occurred in May 2022 to a sizeable coin. And unlike both a Ponzi scheme and a usual pump and dump scheme, the leading crypto is not just redistributive, taking from Peter and giving to Paul. Bitcoin is a deeply negative sum game, owing to the costs of  mining . As a result, in a crash, aggregate losses would outweigh gains by the cumulated cost of mining. Leonardo DiCaprio  and  The Wolf of Wall Street A 2013 Hollywood thriller  about pump and dump  in a boiler shop is  The Wolf of Wall Street . Leonardo DiCaprio plays the wolf; he makes his living—a high one, full of women, booze, drugs, private jets, and his own yacht—by selling penny stocks to the dentists of Newark and Jersey City and Peoria. Leonardo and his subordinates create or buy a shell of a company with an emotive name—Fusion Biometrics might be an example. Initially, they own all of the shares; then they sell a few shares to each other at slightly higher prices, and once they have a track record that shows that the prices increase day after day and week after week, they hustle the dentists and the undertakers and car-wash owners for their orders. Eventually, they sell all the shares to these investors. Their trick or skill is to sell a lot of shares to the public on the basis of the increases in prices that they have managed. And when they have no more shares to sell, they stop buying the shares, and the price falls through the floor when one of the gullible dentists seeks to sell his shares and realize his profits so he can get the money to buy a Ferrari. In a case of life imitating art, the movie was co-produced by the stepson of the Malaysian prime minister and funded with the proceeds of bond sales by a state-owned development agency  in Malaysia  that had been misappropriated by a combination of Goldman Sachs bankers, the prime minister and other officials, and a local fixer, still at large. Goldman Sachs ended up paying a ‘criminal fine and disgorgement’ of $2.9 billion for its role in paying $1.6 billion in bribes, the largest settlement to date under  the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act .* Goldman bankers in the region have been convicted of a crime, but senior management had not enquired very energetically into why the firm received over $600 million to underwrite $6.5 billion of bonds, about ten times the going rate for an investment grade agency bond. *U.S. Department of Justice, ‘Goldman Sachs Charged in Foreign Bribery Case and Agrees to Pay Over $2.9 Billion’,  Justice News , 22 October 2020.  https://​www.​justice.​gov/​opa/​pr/​goldman-sachs-charged-foreign-bribery-case-and-agrees-pay-over-29-billion , accessed June 1, 2022. Minsky-Kindleberger Meets Bitcoin Bitcoin  had a nerdy start. It was first proposed as a ‘peer-to-peer’ means of encrypted payment in a white paper in 2008, complete with 8 references. 4  By making payments expensive, bitcoin could be transferred securely over the internet without the benefit of a financial intermediary and without the benefit of trust. A new technology promised ‘every man a banker.’ This scheme resonated with those upset by the role of banks in the Great Financial Crisis in 2008 and the public support provided to them. Enthusiasts contrasted bitcoin’s limited number to the rapid expansion of major central bank balance sheets at the time. Bitcoin’s  price rose from less than a dollar at its launch in 2009 to $1000 in 2013. Bitcoin graduated from cryptographic esoterica and libertarian dream to financial mania. Investors diffused from the technically adept and ideologically committed to those  with a fear of missing out  (FOMO). Referring to Minsky’s phases of a financial  mania, Joost van der Burgt , visiting the San Francisco Fed from  the Dutch Central Bank , pinpoints the end of 2013, when bitcoin reached $1000, as the displacement—the moment when a new way of making money became apparent. 5  According to van der  Burgt, bitcoin  then entered its boom phase. During the boom, bitcoin attracted an increasing number of imitators, and with the competition new opportunities for the application of leverage to crypto. Of course, free entry raised questions about the selling point of a strictly limited supply of 21  million bitcoin . The most important  imitator, ether , started in 2015 on  the Ethereum  blockchain. Like Avis, this number 2 tries harder. The Ethereum blockchain supports not just transfers  of ether  but also supports automated contracts that execute transactions under certain conditions, so-called smart contracts. Ethereum enabled the development  of so-called decentralized finance  (DeFi) in 2021, bringing lending, borrowing, leverage, and automated trading to crypto 6  (as well as often silly non-fungible tokens—blockchained and transferable evidence of ownership of electronic objects). At its peak, much of the $250 billion of crypto assets ‘locked’—perhaps parked would be the more accurate term—in smart contracts amounted to leverage. Van der Burgt  dates crypto’s entry into its euphoria phase in late 2017, when bitcoin reached $20,000. He noted that classic signs of euphoria, namely taxi drivers talking  about bitcoin  investment and generous use of leverage by investors. A ‘crypto winter’ that saw bitcoin’s price fall by two-thirds between early January 2018 and early February 2018 may question this timing of euphoria. However, its rise from $5000 to $60,000 between mid-March 2020 and March 2021, and its subsequent rise to $69,000 in November 2021, surely  took bitcoin  into euphoria. Euphoria saw the development of crypto’s own money, a development common to manias. The irony is that there was no general shortage: the US dollar money supply had risen hugely above trend owing to the combination of Treasury pandemic transfers to households and the Fed’s buying of Treasury  bonds  in 2020–2021. Yet as crypto trading came to rely on centralized platforms (as described in the next section), it lacked a stable unit to settle trades and serve as collateral. Banks declined to convert crypto into dollars speedily and cheaply owing to constraints like know-your-customer and anti-money laundering rules. So crypto adopted its own dollar stand-ins, persuasively  named stablecoins . These were also coded entries  on blockchains , but their promoters promised to hold their dollar value stable. Liquidity in the crypto ecology, including the novel automated lending and borrowing programs that sprang up in 2021, came to depend  on stablecoins , and their backing with real money, or lack of it, introduced vulnerabilities. As described below, May 2022 saw the crash of the fourth  largest stablecoin , terra , and the total loss of value of an associated  coin, luna , that was intended to secure  the stablecoin’s  value. These crashes shook the conviction  that bitcoin  would recover from its loss of half its value since November 2021. Thus, the May 2022 crashes suggested that crypto euphoria was giving way to distress. Recall from Chapters  2  and  6  that distress denotes the period when some players realize that the door is closing on their ability to exit the object of speculation at a profit and to convert near-money to real money. Bitcoin versus the South Sea Bubble In  2013, Nout Wellink , former head of  the Dutch Central Bank ,  judged bitcoin  as ‘worse than the tulip mania. At least then you got a tulip, now you get nothing.’* Perhaps a different contrast better serves to highlight bitcoin’s extreme nature. The South Sea bubble of 300 years ago was a mania with a government charter. As an anti-institutional  project, bitcoin  could hardly differ more from the South Sea Company. In 1720, Parliament legislated the consolidation of government debt into the South Sea; in 2009, an anonymous group of computer programmers launched bitcoin. A dominant schemer ran the South Sea Company, corrupting politicians, orchestrating its market operations, and self-dealing; to change bitcoin’s code, some combination of core developers, numerous nodes, and numerous miners are the operators. In terms of the functions of money, the South Sea Company consolidated an existing store of value secured by state taxing power; bitcoin was intended as a means of payment and nothing but its supposed usefulness stands behind it. The South Sea Company should have been readily valued, holding government bonds bearing a known interest rate (5 percent then 4 percent) and callable in seven years; bitcoin is nigh-on impossible to value, as a zero coupon perpetual bond, an asset with no maturity and no promised cash flow (formerly a financial joke). The South Sea shares traded in 1720 in a range between 1000 and 100 in the months between hitting its lunatic note in April and collapsing in September; bitcoin between $100 and $70,000 in its long run since 2013. In 1721, after the crash, Parliament not only passed the Act to Restore Publick Credit to override contracts and to apportion gains and losses but also confiscated the estates of the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Company’s directors; it is hard to imagine any legal effort to reapportion gains and losses after a crypto collapse (see below). The South Sea Bubble arguably advanced British public finances by transforming the bulk of public obligations into a more homogeneous and tradeable form. It remains to be seen whether and if the technological innovation spurred by crypto makes a similarly significant and lasting contribution. *Alex Hern, ‘Bitcoin Hype Worse Than “Tulip Mania”, Says Dutch Central Banker’,  The Guardian , 4 December 2013. 
 The Institutionalization of Crypto Bitcoin’s  boom and euphoria phases saw the development of institutions to make the trading of cryptocoins easier. Trading platforms developed to enable the trading of crypto against dollars and crypto against crypto. The convenience of trading crypto against crypto led to the development  of stablecoins  as proxies for the dollar. Contrary to the founding vision, these institutions centralized trading and required trust to operate. As if in a sped-up recapitulation of the history of financial abuses, these institutions operated in a way that seemed almost calculated to lose that trust. A tellingly euphoric moment was the April 2021 initial public offering of crypto trading  platform Coinbase , which mostly  trades bitcoin   and ether  against the dollar. Its price settled on its first trading day at a valuation of $65 billion, within spitting distance of the valuation of the parent of the New York Stock Exchange. 7  This Delaware corporation claimed 6 million monthly transacting users in Q1 2021 (9 million by the first quarter of 2022) and $223 billion of ‘assets on platform.’ 8 This centralization of trading brought conflicts of interest long prohibited in traditional finance.  Although Coinbase  was often described as an exchange, in fact, US states regulated it as a money transmission business. 9  As such, it dealt with its customers as a principal; such transactions represented 11 percent of its revenue in 2020. 10  A proper exchange is not simultaneously a principal. Coinbase is a founder of the consortium that established  the stablecoin   USDC , which it promotes on its trading platform. 11  Coinbase also comingled customer accounts and its own corporate holdings. Only in May 2022 did the SEC finally  require Coinbase  to disclose the implication that customers could end up as the firm’s general creditors in the event of its bankruptcy—centralization with a vengeance. 12 A second trading  platform, Binance , epitomized overtrading. Here highly leveraged  derivative bitcoin  trades came to drive prices in spot trading of bitcoin versus the dollar as conducted on Coinbase. In the first quarter of 2021, when bitcoin doubled in price from $30,000 to $60,000, a so-called perpetual swap contract for bitcoin averaged over $20 billion in turnover a day  on Binance , about 20 times the spot trading  on Coinbase . 13  Traders use this contract to take a leveraged position  in bitcoin , putting down only a small fraction of their bet and settling gains or losses in crypto. After a flash crash in May 2021, when China prohibited financial institutions from dealing in crypto, the  unregulated Binance  announced the reduction of its maximum leverage from 100 or more to 20 times, still very high for an extremely volatile asset, but actual practice is not clear. 14  The upshot is an inverted triangle of highly leveraged bets that drive the prices on the relatively narrow foundation of bitcoin-dollar trades. Thus, price discovery for crypto takes place on an unregulated platform that features high leverage.  Moreover, Binance  is said to have turned a blind eye to billions in illicit flows of funds well into 2021. 15  The institutionalization of crypto leaves its liquidity and price at the mercy of events in such a venue. The largest crypto exchange depends on the  largest stablecoin . Most of  the bitcoin  trades  on Binance  are perpetual swaps of bitcoin against the leading  stablecoin, tether . It is easy to see why a dollar stand-in would be useful in this key derivatives market. If a trade of crypto against the dollar cannot use the dollar to post margin or to settle gains and losses, it is awkward to use the volatile bitcoin for these purposes. It is much more convenient to use the stable leg of the trade to post margin and to settle gains and losses than to use the highly volatile leg for these purposes. For an unregulated exchange that does not have good access to the dollar, an ersatz dollar is very useful. More  broadly, stablecoins  became a useful vehicle currency in the crypto world and extended its reach. A trader  selling bitcoin  and looking to buy again or to switch into another crypto coin could avoid the delays and expense of acquiring and then selling dollars. In DeFi transactions, using smart contracts, i.e., coded instructions running on  the Ethereum   blockchain , rather than financial institutions, stablecoins can be lent out and borrowed at interest rates well above those on the corresponding dollars. By October 2021, the aggregate value  of stablecoins  weighed in at $127 billion, with market leader tether amounting to over half of this sum. 16  This was just 3 percent of the value of outstanding cryptocoins. Despite the decline in the value of crypto overall in 2022, stablecoins reached an aggregate measured value of $180 billion at the end of February 2022 17  and held around that level into May. 18  Though still a small share of crypto market value, they play a key role in the crypto universe: the turnover  of tether  in particular exceeds that  of bitcoin   and ether  combined. As the roles  of Coinbase , Binance ,  and stablecoins  have grown, the ‘peer-to-peer’ vision of the founders of bitcoin has dropped by the wayside. Partly this resulted from a design that sacrificed an efficient means of payment for a trustless, non-institutional  system. Bitcoin  proved by design pretty clunky when payment traffic turned heavy; transactions slowed and congestion led to higher transfer fees. A payments network should be ‘the more the merrier,’  but bitcoin  proved to be ‘the more the sorrier’ at its local price peak in late 2017. 19 Decentralization thus gave way to a centralization appropriate to a heavily traded speculative would-be store  of value. By mid-2021, cryptocurrency  exchanges and trading desks were estimated to be responsible for 80 percent of transactions on  the bitcoin   blockchain  and about a third of holdings. 20 Ideologically, the recruits to crypto investing did not share any libertarian  vision. Rafael Auer   and David Tercero-Lucas  analyzed a survey by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta and found that bitcoin holders did not stand out in their dissatisfaction with the standard financial system. 21 But the institutionalization of crypto introduced vulnerabilities into its world. Problems at the two trading  platforms, Coinbase   and Binance , could lead investors to re-evaluate the value of crypto  investing. Stablecoins  made a very specific promise and under the best of management would still face the risk of runs. If the major stablecoins were to become unusable, crypto liquidity would be impaired, pushing down prices, and DeFi, which runs on stablecoins, could fall apart. If tether  were as well managed as a regulated money market fund it could still find itself losing money on an investment, ‘breaking the buck’ (i.e., reporting a share value below $1) and suffering a run, as did  the Reserve Primary Fund  in 2008. Then the Fed and US Treasury backstopped money market funds to limit the fallout. Even without any fund’s breaking the buck in March 2020, regulated money market funds suffered runs and again the Fed rode to the rescue. But there is ample reason to suppose  that tether  is not managed with the prudence of a standard money market fund. In early 2021, the New York State Attorney General fined the firm, accusing it of falsely claiming that its liabilities were fully backed by dollars, and required it to disclose its holdings. 22  Outrage greeted tether’s first disclosure—a circle chart of its holdings in March 2021. 23  An SEC-regulated money market fund, by contrast, periodically discloses all of its holdings at the level of security. Tether  is a ‘company that seemed to be practically quilted out of red flags’, 24  concluded a  Business Week  cover story in October 2021. But the crypto world continued to rely on it. Remarkably, a leading business glossy shouted fire, but the crowded theatre’s patrons just remained in their seats. For over a year guesses as to the obligors and nature  of tether’s  reported holdings  of commercial paper  ranged widely. Was it paper issued by distressed Chinese real estate  developers? IOUs backed by cryptocurrencies ? Or worse? In October 2022, Tether Holdings claimed that it had run its commercial paper holdings that back tether to zero. But as of 30 September 2022 it reported that 9% of the assets backing tether consisted of tether-denominated loans, that is, IOUs secured by undisclosed assets, likely cryptocurrencies. These could make the Lehman  Brothers commercial paper  that led to the run on  the Reserve Primary Fund  in September 2008 look solid. Since tether pays no interest and Treasury bills yielded 3% in September 2022, tether could make billions in annual profit without making such loans, leaving observers scratching their heads. In May 2022, the unpegging of a  minor stablecoin  (terra) and the collapse of an associated $40 billion plus cryptocoin (luna) in weeks signaled the possibility of the onset of distress. At this stage, the inflow of new investors slows, and some current investors look to liquidate holdings and raise real dollar cash. 
 From Terra to Luna and Back The unpegging of a  minor stablecoin  in May 2022 and the associated collapse of a widely held cryptocoin highlighted the risk posed by stablecoins to the crypto ecology and the potential of a widely held cryptocoin to ‘go to zero.’ Their  creator, Do Kwon , promoted terra (UST) as a stablecoin maintained by an algorithm rather than backed, as  with tether , by a more or less sufficient portfolio of more or less liquid assets. The algorithmic approach was sold as better, even more pure, in its lack of reliance on an institution. After all, if a  backed stablecoin  has a foot in traditional finance, the authorities could freeze its assets. The idea was a fine piece of financial engineering to produce stability out of instability.  If terra  were to trade below $1 par value, a trader could buy it with a real dollar (or more likely tether) and exchange it for a dollar’s worth  of luna , whatever luna’s price. At $100 per luna, one terra would fetch a hundredth of a luna; at $10 per luna,  one terra  would fetch a tenth of a luna. Then the luna could be sold for dollars (or tether) and the trader could in principle pocket the gap between terra’s price and par. The short and the long of it was that the algorithm would enable arbitrage to  support terra’s  stable value at $1—if there were always a market bid for  the luna . Yet potential buyers would know that as much luna as necessary would be issued. The  algorithmic stablecoin’s  parallel in traditional finance carried the telling Wall Street adjective, ‘death-spiral’(box). 25 ‘Death spiral’ preferred shares and par reset junk bonds Algorithmic stablecoins are cousins to two other clever pieces of financial engineering. A ‘death spriral’ convertible is a bond or preferred share sold as a fixed-income investment that, at maturity, converts into the common equity in the firm. However, the bond is converted not into a fixed number of shares, but into as many shares as are required to preserve the bond’s par value. If the firm is in distress, the prospect of a massive dilution of the equity-holders’ claim on the firm can lead the equity price to collapse—hence the name. Another similar fine piece of financial engineering featured in the largest leveraged buyout in the 1980s. Par reset junk bonds formed part of KKR’s 1989 buyout of RJR Nabisco. The coupon on these junk bonds was to be periodically reset to bring the securities to par. The worse the bonds were doing, the higher the coupon. Once RJR Nabisco’s finances became distressed, an interest rate that would bring the bonds to par would bankrupt the company. Only KKR bringing new equity to the deal prevented the firm’s finances from blowing up.* * Robert N. McCauley,  Judith S. Ruud   and Frank Iacono ,  Dodging Bullets  (Cambridge: MIT Press, 1999), chapter 4. The stakes were not  small. Terra  had joined the top four  of stablecoins   and luna  the top ten rank of cryptocoins. Demand for terra was turbocharged by a 19 percent interest rate paid by a smart contract  called Anchor  controlled  by Do Kwon . (As  with much ‘decentralized finance ,’ in this case, decentralized governance was an illusion.) Terra’s growth seemed to provide a (spurious) argument for holding the linked luna. On April 5, luna’s price had risen to $116, up from 63 cents on 1 January 2021, and its market cap had reached $41 billion, 26  and outstanding terra had climbed to UST 17 billion (then trading near par and so worth $17 billion). 27  Thus the whole complex had reached a value of almost $60 billion, ostensibly on the promise of the uses  for terra   and luna  under development, but mostly on the basis of the 19 percent promised on terra and a price trend for luna pointing to the moon. Terra  found little use as a means of payment, and by Friday 6 May UST14 billion of UST 18 billion was parked at the Anchor  protocol earning 19 percent. 28  As the  Financial Times  quoted the author just before the run on terra, ‘When you hear of a 9 or 19 percent short-term interest rate on an asset [stablecoin] that is supposed to have a stable value against the dollar, put your hand on your wallet.’ 29 The run started over the weekend, with holders of terra withdrawing UST 2 billion or more per day  from Anchor  on Sunday through Thursday. The conversion of UST at par  to luna  was limited (‘gated’) to a certain amount per day, and sales on exchanges  saw terra  slump to a discount. The day-by-day number of  outstanding luna  provides summary statistics of the crash. In the week ending Friday 6 May, there were 343 million outstanding luna as the price fell from the $80s to the $60s. Outstanding luna rose 9 percent on 10 May, then almost quadrupled to 1.5 billion on 11 May.  Outstanding luna  gained two zeros to reach 169 billion on 12 May and the printing stopped at 6.5 trillion on the lucky 13th of May. 30  Four zeros had been added to the number of Luna outstanding in four days in a brief and spectacularly unsuccessful defence of terra’s peg to the dollar. Luna fell to a rounding error away from zero and was delisted from  exchanges. Terra  hit 15 cents on Friday the 13th, and subsequently traded lower; UST 11 billion  remained. Luna  became worthless before half of the terra had been converted. 31 In the weeks before the  run, Do Kwon  had sought to defend his creation by selling luna to buy $3.5 billion-worth  of bitcoin . Practically, the downward trend of bitcoin prices undermined this would-be defence. Conceptually, the purchase undermined the argument for the algorithmic approach. In any case, the sale of  the bitcoin  did more to spread the selling to bitcoin than to  rescue terra . Questions remain whether the sales of bitcoin against terra favored insiders. The question can also be posed regarding how the promoters of terra-luna fared. As noted, at the peak in early April 2022, the value  of terra   and luna  approached $60 billion. Almost all of those who had bought from the promoters were sitting on capital gains on their luna at that peak valuation, so this sum is too high as an estimate of the take of the promoters. One must also take into account that the promoters sold at widely varying  prices. Binance  was reported to have received 15 million luna for its $3 million investment in 2018, which were worth $1.6 billion at the peak. 32  In this case, the promoters only made $3 million. (Binance claims to have held the luna and to have taken the loss.) It is entirely possible that the promoters pocketed $1 billion or more on a venture that a law professor in 2021 dubbed ‘Built to Fail.’ 33  Do Kwon’s  defence is that he thought it could succeed. A widely held coin crashed from over $100 to 0 in five weeks and  a stablecoin  was implicated in the market dynamics. In the immediate wake  of terra’s   unpegging, tether  came under pressure and traded as low as 95 cents on 12 May 2022. It recovered to near par within days, but its reported outstanding amount declined from 83 to 67 billion at the end of June. 34 The demonstration that what had been advertised  by Binance  as a safe asset could tumble in value took its toll on the willingness of investors to lend crypto through DeFi protocols. The total value of coins ‘locked’ on such smart contracts had reached $250 billion—including considerable leverage 35 —around the turn of the year 2021–2022 and had already declined by a fifth by March. 36  From around $200 billion in early May, it reached $75 billion by mid-July and $43 billion in December. 37 The institutional toll from terra/luna contagion spread fast. On 12 June, a crypto borrowing and lending  platform, Celsius , which claimed a million customers who earned 17 percent on over $20 billion in assets in August 2021, froze withdrawals. 38  It has since filed for bankruptcy, along with crypto lending  platform Voyager  and crypto  hedge fund Three Arrows . At issue in the Voyager bankruptcy is the issue that we have highlighted  for Coinbase , namely whether the crypto assets on deposit are held for the customers, or are Voyager’s property. 39 Many of those who had  bought luna  felt like victims, but had a hard time putting their finger on what had befallen  them. Even critics of cryptocurrencies  have had a hard time characterizing them. 
 FTX : Pump and Dump with a Twist In November 2022, the second largest crypto exchange, FTX, declared bankruptcy after suffering a run. A million customers and creditors were left with about $8 billion of losses. Founder  Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF)  saw a peak fortune of $26 billion evaporate, and his lieutenants rapidly pled guilty to federal criminal charges of defrauding customers and misleading investors on SBF's orders. FTX’s new CEO, who liquidated Enron, was shocked to find lemonade stand accounting and emoji controls. Discussion of this crash has ranged from SBF’s dressing and sleeping habits to his political contributions and ‘effective altruism.’ Here the focus is on how a worthless token became cash.  SBF pumped and dumped with a twist. He founded crypto trading firm  Alameda Research  in 2017, and FTX in 2019. That July, FTX created out of nothing its own token called  FTT , which offered holders discounts on FTX fees. FTX minted 350 million FTT, kept half and ‘pre-sold' a fifth before its exchange listing at an average price of 14 cents, raising $10 million. Major holders FTX and Alameda dominated a thin and illiquid market in which FTT traded up from its advertised listing price of $1 to peak price of $80 and a market cap of $10 billion (based on Coinmarketcap’s implied float of 125 million FTT) in September 2021. Alameda seems to have borrowed billions of dollars against FTT collateral from various sources.  Securities and Exchange Commission v. Caroline Ellison and  Zixiau “Gary” Wang   of December 21, 2022 (22-cv-10794, SDNY, paragraph 4) accused the head of Alameda: ‘ Ellison , acting at the direction of Bankman-Fried, engaged in automated purchases of FTT tokens on various platforms in order to increase the price of those tokens and inflate the value of Alameda’s collateral, which allowed Alameda to borrow even more money from external lenders at increased risk to the lenders...’ Then, after the May 2022 collapse of Terra/Luna, Alameda lost access to external loans and repaid them by apparently pledging FTT for loans by FTX of its client assets—dollars, bitcoin, tether, ether. Where, beyond a $1 billion loan to SBF and other loans to FTX executives, the funds went is not clear at writing.  The twist is ingenious. After FTT’s price was pumped up by the FTX ‘bots’, it was not dumped in a myriad of investor phone calls, the usual retail approach. Instead, ‘secured’ borrowing ‘monetized’ FTT: a novel wholesale dump. Ultimately, customers’ misplaced trust in FTX was turned into cash. But along the way was discovered a new (automated) pump and wholesale dump through ‘secured’ borrowing. 
 Worse Than a Ponzi 40 What is bitcoin from an economic perspective? Probably the most frequent answer by skeptics among economists and others is that it is a Ponzi scheme. In early 2021, Brazilian computer  scientist Jorge Stolfi  made the following argument  that Bitcoin  is a Ponzi scheme 41 : 1. Investors buy in the expectation of profits.   2. That expectation is sustained by the profits of those that cash out.   3. But there is no external source for those profits; they come entirely from new investments.   4. And the operators take away a large portion of the money.   
 All of this rings true. Yet in calling it a Ponzi scheme, skeptics are too kind to bitcoin on two counts.  First, bitcoin  makes no promises and cannot have the same endgame as a Ponzi scheme. Second, it is a deeply negative sum game from a broad social perspective. It is unfair to Charles Ponzi to call bitcoin a Ponzi. In 1920, Ponzi promised 50 percent on a 45-day investment and actually paid out to some investors. He suffered and even survived runs before the authorities caught up with him. The scheme did not last a year because of the extravagant return, but Ponzi made a promise, paid some initial returns, and suffered runs. In the largest and probably the longest running Ponzi scheme in history, Bernie Madoff paid returns of around 1 percent a month. He offered to cash out his scheme’s participants, both the original sum ‘invested’ and the ‘return’ thereon. As a result, the scheme could and did suffer a run; the Great Financial Crisis of 2008 led to a cascade of redemptions by participants and the scheme’s collapse. But the resolution has extended beyond its collapse on account of remarkable and ongoing legal proceedings. These have outlived Madoff himself, who died in early 2021. Many are unaware that a bankruptcy trustee,  Irving H. Picard , has doggedly and successfully pursued those who took more money out of the scheme than they put in. He even managed to follow the money into offshore dollar accounts, litigating a controversial extraterritorial reach of US law all the way to the US Supreme Court. 42  Of the $20 billion in recognized original investments in the scheme (which the victims had been told had reached a value more than three times that sum), some $14 billion, a striking 70 percent, has been recovered and distributed. 43  Claims of up to $1.6 million are being fully repaid. By contrast to investments with Madoff, bitcoin is bought not as an income-earning asset but rather as a zero coupon perpetual. In other words, it promises nothing as a running yield and never matures with a required terminal payment. It follows that it cannot suffer a run. The only way a holder  of bitcoin  can cash out is by a sale to someone else. Bitcoin’s collapse would look very different from that of Ponzi’s or Madoff’s scheme. As noted above, one possible trigger could be the collapse of a  big stablecoin ; other possible triggers lurk in the trading platforms. Given their record, the lack of regulation and scant disclosure, it is not hard to imagine a big stablecoin persistently breaking the buck. This could so disrupt the whole ecology of crypto that there could be no bids  for bitcoin . The market might close indefinitely. In this event, there would be no long-running legal effort to chase down those who cashed in their bitcoin early in order to redistribute their profits to those left holding bitcoins. Holders  of bitcoin  would have no claim on those who bought early and sold. In its cash flow, bitcoin resembles a penny  stock pump and dump  scheme 44  more than a Ponzi scheme. In a pump and dump scheme, traders acquire basically worthless stock, talk it up and perhaps trade it among themselves at rising prices before unloading it on those drawn in by the chatter and the price action. Like  the pump and dump  scheme, bitcoin taps into the pure desire for capital gains. Buyers cannot stand the sight of friends getting rich overnight: they suffer  an acute fear of missing out  (FOMO). In any  case, bitcoin  makes no promises and cannot end as a Ponzi scheme ends in a run. This is not to say that Ponzi schemes of varying sophistication do not abound in crypto and DeFi. In the terra-luna scheme, inflows into terra chasing the 19 percent interest pushed up the price  of luna , sales of which funded the 19 percent return, according  to Binance’s  founder and head Changpeng Zhao. 45  His after-the-fact description is ironic in view of Binance’s having advertised  the terra  investment as a ‘safe and happy’ opportunity. 46  In any case, here was a return promise, more generous than Madoff’s in a lower interest rate environment, and a story for a stable principal as well. One can think of this scheme as a Ponzi scheme grafted onto the standard  crypto pump and dump . The other big difference between bitcoin and a Ponzi scheme is that the former is, from an aggregate or social standpoint, a negative sum game. To the extent that real resources are used up to  make bitcoin  run, it is costly in a way that Madoff’s two- or three-man operation was not. (This was also true of ether up until September 2022, when it converted from its energy-intensive mining [‘proof of work’] to a more environmentally friendly means [‘proof of stake’] of keeping its participants honest.) From the social standpoint, what Madoff took out of his scheme and finally consumed is a redistribution in a zero-sum game (the trustee sold  his penthouse). Stolfi’s  fourth observation above, ‘the operators take away a large portion of the money’ lumps together Madoff’s take and bitcoin’s miners’ revenues, but these are very different in economic terms. With bitcoin, the game is to name the country whose electricity consumption equals that of all the puzzle-solvers (miners) who get to effect transactions and  receive bitcoin  in reward. Even if the electricity were priced to include its contribution to global warming (its ‘environmental externality’)—which presumably it mostly is not—this represents a real cost. How big a cost? At the beginning  of 2021, Stolfi  put the cumulative payments to bitcoin’s miners since 2009 at $15 billion. 47  At the then price of bitcoin, he put the increase in cost at about $10 million per day, which mostly pays for electricity. At  higher bitcoin  prices in the 'teens of thousand dollars, the hole is growing faster. About 900 new bitcoin a day require most of $20 million a day in electricity and computer wear and tear. Thus, the negative sum in the bitcoin game is in tens of billions of dollars and rising at most of a billion dollars per month. If the price  of bitcoin  collapses to zero, the gains of those who sold would fall short of the losses of holders by this growing sum. To liken bitcoin to a Ponzi scheme or even to  a pump and dump  scheme, both basically redistributive, is to flatter bitcoin. Bitcoin  is a long-running,  decentralized pump and dump  scheme with a negative sum. True, there are many early investors with an interest in new investors (although recent research points to much more concentration among early miners than previously thought 48 ), rather than a  single ‘Wolf of Wall Street ,’ the real-life pumper and dumper  played by Leonardo DiCaprio . True, they are more likely to sport beards than slicked-back hair. True, many are sincere in their belief that trustless transfers or stateless money will somehow contribute to human happiness. But it must be said that, since bitcoin, promoters of coins commonly allocate coins at the outset to insiders, ranging from 15 percent  for Ethereum  to about 50 percent  for Binance . 49   Since bitcoin , crypto promoters are openly ‘talking their own books.’ And true, it is  a pump and dump  of a remarkably shambolic character. An industry source has estimated on the basis of inactivity that some one-fifth of bitcoin is held, if that is the right word, by those who have lost their codes. 50  One regretful holder sought to have a public dump in South Wales dug up to find his discarded laptop with his codes for 3000 bitcoin. 51 To conclude, an economic analysis  of bitcoin  finds it unique in the history of manias. As an object of speculation, bitcoin is unprecedented in the degree to which there is no there there. This post-modern mania features big prices for entries on nobody’s spreadsheet. A zero coupon perpetual has arrived not as a joke but as a trillion-dollar asset. Unlike a Ponzi scheme, bitcoin cannot end in a run. However, the centralized institutions that have grown up to accommodate mass investment  in bitcoin  and others could fail investors and precipitate a crash. In a crash, the holders  of bitcoin  will have no one to pursue to recover what they invested. Unlike a Madoff-style Ponzi scheme, early investors who get out before the crash need not fear that a court will demand their winnings. Collectively, the losses will exceed gains by what investors cumulatively paid the miners for bitcoin. This sum has gone up in smoke, a social loss. The holders  of bitcoin  and other crypto might in the end only wish it had been a Ponzi scheme. Play to Earn Developers of cryptocoins are on the lookout for ‘use cases,’ and gaming is a natural use. The pitch to those who play normal games on their cell phones is, ‘Why not earn while you play?’. For a  time, Axie Infinity  was the biggest online crypto video game. Its promise was to make work and play become one. Its achievement was millions of low-income players working on gaming as a cottage industry and paying away much of their earnings to the owners of the gaming tools. Its rise had much in common with that of terra-luna: it offered unsustainable rewards to players that propelled growth. In both cases, one can think of the rewards as marketing spending, within a business model of bringing money in, thereby building demand for the venture’s main coin, and then selling it at fancy prices. The climax of this game story is not a run, as with terra-luna, but instead the largest hack in DeFi’s short history. By then, the promoters had had plenty of opportunity to unload the venture’s coin on ‘investors’ drawn in by the coin's price rise. The game really took off in April 2021 when its developers moved the game off of  the Ethereum   blockchain  network to avoid its delays and fees owing to the same decentralized, slow, expensive, and energy-intensive validation process as  the Bitcoin  network uses.* The game’s developers opted for nine trusted validators to authorize deposits and withdrawals into and out of the game of number two coin ether (ETH)  or Coinbase’s   stablecoin (USDC ). In the game, players use at least three digital pets called Axies to compete in battles. ‘The monsters are cartoonish blobs distinguished by their unique mixture of interchangeable parts, not unlike Mr. Potato Head.’** So far, this is like the 1990s video game Pokémon, but there are two twists. The first twist is that players must buy these Axies, non-fungible tokens (NFTs) with varying battle strengths. At the peak of the game’s growth in mid-2021, three Axies cost the equivalent of hundreds of dollars, or even a thousand dollars for more potent ones. First, pay to play,  then play to earn . In Fig.  14.1 , in the left three columns, dollars are converted  to ether , then bridged onto  the Axie Infinity   blockchain  (‘Ronin’) and are used to purchase Axies. A text document depicts the axie infinity blockchain, which includes conversion of dollar to ether and incorporated into the axie infinity blockchain to purchase axies used to play games to get S L P and A X S as reward points that are again used to purchase axies and play games or can be converted to ether and back into dollars. Fig. 14.1 Axie Infinity flow of funds ( Note  Axie = non-fungible token (NFT), digital pet used to play game; ETH = ether; AXS = Axie Shards, main ‘governance’ coin; SLP = Smooth Love Potion, in-game reward coin; USDT = tether stablecoin.  Source  Authors’ elaboration) The second twist is that successful players earn an in-game coin, known—why not?—as smooth love potions (SLPs) as well as Axie Shards (AXS). AXS is the game’s main coin, shown in Fig.  14.1  in the column ‘Play Game.’ These can be ‘cashed’ out of the game in the last column in Fig.  14.1  by moving them to  the Binance  exchange, exchanging them for tether (USDT) and selling  the tether  for US dollars. Or, remaining in the column ‘Play Game,’ the coins can be used to ‘breed’ new Axies, starting with two extant Axies. A newly bred Axie can be taken to the Axie market and sold to new players or old players looking to step up their game, with a 4.25 percent transaction fee paid to the game’s treasury, controlled by AXS holders. Given this need for SLPs and AXS to breed Axies, new players created a demand for the winnings of the current players. In sum, take dollars, buy Axies, play with them to earn SLPs and AXS, and then cash them out or use them to breed Axies for sale. With no promises of X percent return or stable Axie values, this is not quite a Ponzi scheme packaged as a video game. Still, players brought real money to the game and hoped to make a return. When new players were bringing in more money than was being cashed out, the prices of Axies, SLP, and AXS rose. The game’s developers and their venture capital backers were playing a game of setting player rewards to recruit new players and their money, generating activity in the game that would draw buyers to AXS. The developers then sold their AXS at elevated prices to ‘investors’ who had no interest in playing the game. Generous player rewards did generate a rapid growth of players. From April 2021, daily active players grew rapidly and reached 2.7 million by November 2021.*** At the peak in growth of new players in July–August 2021, when new players almost tripled, SLPs fetched as much as 35–40 cents, with lots of demand for breeding. Skilled players were quitting their jobs.**** Though the developers resided in Vietnam, perhaps half the players were in the Philippines, with Venezuelans a distant second. Many, perhaps most, players did not have the required upfront money to buy Axies, and virtual sharecropping developed. Impecunious players obtained ‘scholarships,’ under which they would use sponsors’ Axies and pay them a third or a half of their earnings. By September, one sponsor group (a ‘guild’ organized as a ‘decentralized autonomous organization,’ almost  a blockchain  corporation) in the Philippines had most of its $850 million in assets in Axie, and had raised money from US private equity.***** Axie Infinity’s  coin AXS, ostensibly entitling holders to govern the game, rose from $6 in early April 2021 to $160 in November 2021, reaching a market value of almost $10 billion.****** The game’s developers raised $7.5 million from venture capitalists in May 2021, and $152 million in October 2021, the latter valuing the startup at $3 billion. But as growth slowed and the rewards stayed generous, inflation set in. By September, players were earning SLPs at twice the rate that they were using them to breed new Axies; their cashing out pushed the SLP price down into the 5- to 10-cent range. The developers severely tightening the terms on which SLPs are earned and spent in February 2022, but their price still fell to a cent or two.******* At this rate, players could not earn the minimum wage in the Philippines and the number of daily players fell by about half. Thieves broke into this already very troubled game on March 23, 2022. Hackers lifted over $600 million dollars worth of ETH  and USDC  held in the game’s stash on  the Ethereum  network. The game designers had cut corners and depended on only nine trusted validators for withdrawals rather than the thousands for Ethereum  or Bitcoin   blockchains  and the hackers were able to compromise five of them. On May 6, the US Treasury identified the hackers as a group linked to North Korea as it sanctioned a crypto-mixing service that obfuscated the origin and destination of crypto transfers for the hackers.******** Amazingly, despite an evident lack of attention to security, private equity backers, led by crypto  exchange Binance , stumped up $150 million in May 2022 to pay back gamers, who owned two-thirds of the $600 million stolen.********* The market capitalization of the AXS coin fell to $1 billion, embodying the hope that players could be compensated fully and the developers could figure out how to make play-to-earn work. Stepping back, a high price of AXS depended on the game’s success in drawing players, activity, and money. Somewhat like the developers of terra-luna, unsustainably high rewards drove very rapid growth. Thanks to the digital sharecropping, the game excited potential buyers of AXS with the idea of introducing millions of people of modest means to the world of crypto wallets, exchanges and so on. The game only flourished for some months. But perhaps it lasted long enough for the developers and the more astute venture capitalists to cash out plenty of AXS.        It is time to pull the threads of the argument together. But before we do, there remains one difficult, unanswered question: Does it make a difference if there is no lender of last resort? For one thing, for most of the financial crises covered from 1720 to 2020, both national and international, a lender of last resort did swing into action in response to the pressures of the market—though often protesting all the way. The role was not always dispatched with efficiency, so that a refined analysis would categorize the aftermath of crises not only by the presence or absence of a lender of last resort but also by how well the role was discharged. Second, the aftermath of an economic downturn depends not just on how the crisis was handled but on a host of other variables, especially the factors affecting long-term investment: population growth, the existence of a frontier, demands arising from war, exports, the presence or absence of innovations that are not fully exploited, and the like. A speculative crisis like that of 1847 in England was likely in any event to be pulled quickly back into prosperity by renewed investment in railroads, regardless of whether the Bank of England suspended the Bank Act of 1844 and stood ready to provide liquidity to all borrowers with sound collateral. Despite these difficulties, we are prepared to make the case, tentatively, that a lender of last resort does shorten the business depression that follows financial crisis. The evidence turns mainly on 1720, 1873, 1882 in France, 1890, 1921, and 1929. In none of these was a lender of last resort effectively present. The depressions that followed them were much longer and deeper than others. Those of the 1870s and 1930s were both known as Great Depressions. When a lender of last resort comes to the rescue, even maladroitly, downturn after the panic is seen to be momentary, transient, ephemeral, episodic, slowing the economy down only briefly. Panic marks in many instances the peak of a normal cycle with a recovery period of about two years, but without deeper significance. Not so, it is claimed, with 1720, 1873, 1882 in France, 1890, 1921, and 1929. The South Sea bubble and its collapse in 1720 proved not so economically damaging, perhaps because the Bank of England’s stabilizing role. Carswell contends that the South Sea bubble’s collapse marked an epochal turning point, but he does not address the narrow claim that a lender of last resort shortens the recovery time. 1  In contrast to this view, Schumpeter characterizes the South Sea bubble as nothing more than an excess and breakdown of speculation. 2  Judged by the bankruptcies—220 in 1720, 288 in 1721, and 240 in 1722—the depression ran the normal two-year course. 3  Ashton puts 1722 as the bottom and 1724–1725 as the peak of the next cycle, with a new, milder crisis from October to December 1726. 4  Hoppit  argues that the South Sea bubble did not much disrupt industrial output and overseas trade, although the joint effect of the Mississippi and South Sea bubbles disrupted the foreign-exchange market. 5  One might argue that the Bank of England did in fact act as a lender of last resort in taking over the stock of the South Sea Company. It originally contracted to do so at 400, later reneged when the Bank itself came close to collapsing, and finally converted the stock only a little above the market when South Sea stock had sunk to 135. 6  Hoppit broadens this view: the ‘Bubble’s effect was not generally felt across Britain and Ireland partly because of the symbolic support for the Bank of England from the king and Prince of Wales…, partly because in turn the Bank of England made strenuous efforts to support credit.’ 7 The eighteenth century in France may be more relevant to our claim. There the trauma of the Mississippi bubble and the collapse of John Law’s system slowed down the development of banking and the expansion of industry. Together with the collapse of the assignats during the Directorate in the 1790s, it made the French neurotic, or even paranoid, about banking for years-just as the Germans were rendered paranoid about inflation by the inflation of 1923 and the British about unemployment after their experiences during the 1920s. We are left then with 1873, 1882 in France, 1890, 1921, and 1929. There was no lender of last resort in 1873 in Vienna, Berlin, and New York, the storm centers of the crash. In London there was no panic, hence no need for a lender of last resort. The French let the Union Générale go to the wall in 1882 with minimal intervention. In 1929, the lender of last resort function was inadequately performed in New York (as suggested earlier, though the verdict does not command general agreement), and in 1931, international operations to halt the spread of collapse and the decline of prices and to restore business confidence were notoriously feeble. On every other occasion from 1763 to 1914, more or less effective steps were taken. It would be helpful if one could discriminate carefully between the rescue operations, to determine which were more and which less adroit and to compare them separately with the length, depth, and width of the depressions that followed. Unhappily, we discriminate only crudely, if at all, limiting the analysis to whether recovery was fast or slow. There can be little doubt that the depression of the 1870s was severe. After 1857 and 1866 (1864 in France), prices declined for two years and then picked up. After 1873, however, they declined for six years to 1879. 8  In the United States there was a severe recession through 1874 and then five long years of severe depression. 9  This would appear to support the hypothesis. But one is given pause by an explicit statement in McCartney that this was the result primarily of a breakdown in basic industries, rather than the disruption of financial machinery. 10  There is no need to identify the entire ‘Great Depression’ from 1873 to 1896 with the absence of lenders of last resort in Berlin, Vienna, and New York—at least one writer doubts whether it was a depression at all rather than merely profitless prosperity. 11  Our inclination, however, is to associate the extended depression of the 1870s in Central Europe, in the United States, and by propagation in Britain with the sharpness of the collapse of prices and the absence of a lender of last resort. This is far from an irrefutable case. In 1882, in France, the speculative banks of Lyons were allowed to fail, with only limited assistance to mitigate some of the disastrous consequences for the brokers who had supported the speculators. Recovery in France was long drawn out, conditioned partly by the slowness of recovery in Britain, the United States, and most of the Continent. 12 The 1890 Baring crisis can be classified either way, either as having or as lacking a lender of last resort. For Britain, there was the equivalent of a domestic lender, that is, the guarantee of the Baring Brothers liabilities, and an international rescue committee, organized by William Lidderdale, the loans from the Bank of France and the State Bank of Russia, plus the latter's commitment not to withdraw its deposit. But for the world outside Europe, there was no such therapy, and the depression was deep and long, lasting until 1896. The troubles of 1890 in  Argentina, Brazil ,  and Chile  were echoed in 1893  in Australia  and the United States, 13  with little or no intentional help from abroad. There was, however, a  deus ex machina . The product of serendipity rather than design, the rapid rise of gold production  in South Africa  followed the discoveries of 1886 in the Rand. The contrast in the response of the world economy to gold discoveries in 1849 and 1851 on one hand and 1886 on the other is striking. In the middle of the century, the Californian and Australian gold strikes were quickly translated into a boom in Europe; in the 1890s, there was no such rapid response. The difference lay in external circumstances: buoyant in the early 1850s, depressed from 1890. The surge of gold production finally produced an effect after 1896, however, serving as a lender of last resort by pouring high-powered money into the system. In the United States, for example, gold coin in circulation rose from $374 million in 1890 to $495 million in 1894 and $679 million in 1899, over a period when US production rose only from $33 million to $79 million, a large increase in terms of percentage, but a modest one in absolute terms and as compared with the rise in circulation. 14 In 1920 and 1921, there was no lender of last resort because the recession was deliberately engineered—by Britain, as a step on the route back to the gold standard, and by the Federal Reserve System in the United States, in order to halt inflation. The United States recovered ‘fairly quickly,’ but the abrupt fall in prices and output in Britain ‘hastily spread to a number of other highly industrial countries and developed into a depression of extreme severity and duration.’ 15  Pedersen  speaks of ‘the quasi-permanent depression inaugurated in 1920,’ although he does not associate the extent of the decline with the absence of a lender of last resort, and he allows, as he should, for the importance attached by the British authorities to a return to gold. He blames the American authorities, however, for deflationary policies that prevented European countries from returning to gold: The authorities seem to have been guided by a somewhat vague idea that conditions were unsound, that prices were too high, that the budget should be balanced, that things would not correct themselves, and that some action ‘cleaning up’ the aftermath of the unsound wartime policy was necessary. Now it is my thesis that this state of mind and the action which it engendered was fateful, because so much depended on the policy carried out in the U.S.A …. … For these reasons I think it safe to conclude that the U.S.A. monetary authorities by stimulating demand in the spring of 1920 instead of contracting it could have prevented the permanent depression of the countries struggling to return to gold, mitigated inflation in a number of countries, and made the attempt of monetary reconstruction of the countries easier, and diminished the structural fall in the prices of primary and agricultural products. 16 
 The argument that the depression of the 1930s was exacerbated by the lack of effective lenders of last resort-domestically in 1929 in the United States, worldwide in 1931—has been dealt with at length above, in a number of places. This evidence through the 1930s by no means constitutes a conclusive demonstration that intervention of a lender of last resort in a panic softens the depression that follows. Too many other factors are at work, both long and short term, and the occasions when a panic has been allowed to run its course are so few that the material is not abundant enough for strong conclusions. At most there remains a presumption, but perhaps not a strong one, that halting a cumulative deflation helps shorten the depression that follows. The major crises in the forty-plus years since this book was originally published have featured some version of the lender of last resort, generally criticized for doing too much and too little. Warts and all, it is a reasonable judgment that the subsequent recovery would generally have been slower in its absence. The aftermath of the Mexican crisis of 1982 echoes in some ways that of the 1890 Baring crisis. Big creditor country banks avoided insolvency and creditor countries enjoyed an economic recovery in the early 1980s, but the borrowing countries recovered slowly. The analogy breaks down in the innovative international lender of last resort operations for Latin American and other debtor countries, which had no parallel in 1890. Going beyond IMF lending with conditions attached, creditor country officials managed commercial bank lending, leaning on commercial banks to stump up ‘new money.’ 17  Latin American debtors used the new money, along with IMF and other official funding and trade surpluses, to service their (rescheduled) bank debt. This management supported borrowers’ growth by maintaining international trade credit, although Mexico still endured a prolonged growth setback. 18  Creditor banks avoided depositor runs and government takeover and worked their way back to solvency, but a more balanced conditionality might have precluded their paying dividends along the way. In the Asian financial crisis, the much-criticized international lender of last resort operations set up a generally solid export-led recovery in the debtor countries. On the creditor side, the Asian financial crisis only slowed the upswing that continued until the bursting of the Dot.com bubble in 2000. The IMF drew criticism for treating the problem in Asia initially as more one of overspending than an international run on fragile structures of debt. 19  After announcements of large public loan packages failed to keep banks from exiting, in Korea, creditor officials led by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York eventually leaned on the banks to roll over short-term credits. 20  On the creditor side, the stakes were generally lower in the Asian financial crisis, with major banks more modestly exposed than they had been in the 1980s in Latin America. That said, Japanese banks’ struggle with their post-crisis bad loans was coming to a slow climax as the Asian financial crisis hit, so there was potential for vicious circles that the last resort lending forestalled. With hindsight, the 4th edition of this book argued prematurely  that Japan’s  weak recovery after the bursting of the bubble in 1990 might count against the efficacy of the lender of last resort there. The 4th edition suggested that the poor recovery might reflect ‘how well the role was discharged’: Japan’s ‘efforts at salvage were slow, widely spaced, and caught up in political maneuvering’ 21 —all points well-taken. The authorities finally stepped up to the plate in 1997–1998 to support a troubled bank and a securities firm and to nationalize two banks. In 1999, the government injected preferred shares across the major banks. 22  To be sure, the Japanese lender of last resort had none of the speed, decisiveness, and democratic buy-in of the Nordic lenders of last resort in 1990–1992. 23  But given the immense scale of the Japanese bubble, in retrospect, the economy performed respectably when account is taken of the evolution of its working-age population.  Economist Paul Krugman , once a sharp critic of Japanese policy-making after the burst of the bubble, quipped after the 2008 Great Financial Crisis that he owed the Japanese emperor an apology for his criticism. 24 The major argument regarding 2008 is whether the lender of last resort should have been more inclusive by saving Lehman Brothers, thereby making the subsequent global decline in economic activity less severe and the recovery more robust. The 7th edition of this book devoted a chapter to Lehman that argued that the decline in employment and GDP and the increase in the fiscal deficit owing to its failure well exceeded the plausible cost of rescuing it. 25  Lawrence Ball  argues at length that the Fed could have rescued Lehman, but did not do so because of political considerations and because of a failure to understand the cost of the failure. 26  Ball claims that without the Lehman collapse ‘the whole Great Recession wouldn’t have been so great.’ 27 However one interprets Lehman, the domestic lender of last resort—re-starting within days of the Lehman collapse—and the international lender of last resort arguably prevented a far worse outcome in 2008. ‘The counterfactual of how the system would have adjusted without the swap lines is too grim to contemplate,’ write three ex-officials who were directly involved. 28  As argued by policymakers Ben  Bernanke, Timothy Geithner ,  and Hank Paulson in  Firefighting: The Financial Crisis and Its Lessons , which includes cameo appearances by Kindleberger and Minsky, the whole Great Recession could have been the Great Depression. 29 The tentative judgment is that domestic and international lender of last resort operations promoted a stronger recovery from  the Covid  recession of 2020. The argument is whether the scale of the fiscal response, particularly in the United States under two presidents, and the two-year persistence of ultra-easy monetary policy, overdid stimulus and stoked global inflation. Does the Lender of Last Resort Forestall Crises? A wider claim is made for lenders of last resort that they make it possible to avoid financial crises altogether. The record shows that financial crises were less frequent in Britain after 1866: 141 years separated the retail run on Northern Rock in 2007 from that on Overend Gurney in 1866. 30  And in the United States, a half of a century separated 1929–1931 from the Mexican default of 1982. In addition, the record can be interpreted to reveal that crises were less terrifying. History is full of hyperbolic statements about the various crises: 1772  Britain: ‘One of the fiercest financial storms of the century.’ 31 1825  Britain: 'A panic seized upon the public such had never been witnessed before.’ 32 1837  United States: ‘One of the most disastrous [panics] this nation ever experienced.’ 33 1847  Britain: ’In the last nine months more reckless and hazardous speculation than any other known in modern times.’ 34 1847  Britain: ‘It may safely be affirmed, that since the fall of Napoleon, the City has never been in a state of greater excitement.’ 35 1857  Britain: ‘Crisis of 1857 the most severe that England or any other nation has ever encountered.’ 36 1857  Hamburg: ‘So complete and classic a panic has never been seen before as now in Hamburg.’ 37 1857  Hamburg: Panic ‘of a violence hitherto unknown.’ 38 1866  Britain: ‘Crisis of 1866 most serious in modern times.’ 39 1866  Britain: ‘Wilder than any since 1825.’ 40 1873  Germany: ’In 56 years, no such protracted crisis.’ 41 1882  France: ‘Never have I seen an equal catastrophe.’ 42 1929  United States: ‘The greatest cycle of speculative boom and collapse in modern times—since, in fact, the South Sea Bubble.’ 43 2008  United States: ‘The worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.’ 44 
 This rhetoric mostly moderated after 1866 in Britain. Consistent with the decline in hyperbole, the view was put forward by a group of distinguished economists in the 1930s that the existence of a lender of last resort, while it may exacerbate overtrading, calms anxieties when overtrading occurs. In July 1932, the Committee on Economic Information, a high-powered group consisting of  Sir Josiah Stamp  (as chairman), G.  D. H. Cole , J.M. Keynes,  Sir Alfred Lewis ,  Sir Arthur Salter ,  Sir Frederick Leith-Ross , with  H. D. Henderson  and  A. F. Hemming  as joint secretaries, wrote the following: As the [19th] century wore on, the knowledge that the Bank Act would be suspended in case of need, and that, as a consequence, harassed debtors with good security to offer would be able to obtain advances from the Bank, sufficed to prevent panics from arising. 45 
 This group of economists, advising the British cabinet, was advocating an international lender of last resort and may have exaggerated the effectiveness of suspending the Bank Act. The committee further seemed to overlook the fact that suspension of the Bank Act had not been a certainty, as Lidderdale went to great length to demonstrate in 1890, concerned as he was about the subversive effects of continuous suspensions. This view that manias were moderating was fairly persuasive in the decades after World War II up to the 1970s. Putting aside 1970s speculation in real estate, farmland, and oil production, the mania for syndicated bank loans to developing countries that figured prominently in the first edition of this book in 1978 suggested that manias had not become historical curiosities. The Japanese mega-bubble marked the 1980s and the Asian financial crisis  marked the 1990s. Talk among macroeconomists of the ‘great moderation’ at the beginning of the present century exploded in 2007–2008. It is hard to avoid the conclusion that the succession of last resort operations in the 1980s, 1990s, and 2000s does not calm anxieties when  the Minsky moment  hits, though many worry that it exacerbates overtrading. A particular version of the question whether the lender of last resort forestalls crises is why the successful use of central  bank  swaps in 2007–2009 did not make their use unnecessary in 2020. The first answer is the botched nature of ‘reform’ of money market funds after the runs on them in 2008. But the second answer is that the Fed’s extension of credit through central bank swaps stirred political controversy at home that undermined the force of the precedent. The ‘reform’ of money market funds left them still exposed to shareholder runs without a standing lender of last resort. In March 2020, firms seeking to raise cash in the face of a possible collapse of revenues took little comfort from the reform’s tweaking of money funds’ liquidity requirements. Worse, the reform mandated that, in the face of extreme demand from shareholders for cash, limits, or ‘gates,’ be applied to  redemptions. Limits excite , and the prospect of such limits accelerated the run. When $150 billion took flight from the funds in days in March 2020, a run on the dollar funding of non-US bans was the mechanical result. In responding to this run, a non-US bank borrowing, hoarding, or lending dollars had to reckon the likelihood of the swap lines being fully reactivated in size and frequency. Here the question was not a legal one. The Congress had in its post-crisis Dodd-Frank Act limited the Fed’s use of its emergency lending powers at home, requiring that the US Treasurer approve and that the Fed target the credit to a class of borrowers and not a single firm. 46  However, Dodd-Frank had not touched the Fed’s ability to offer swap lines. And indeed, in early 2020 the Fed had permanent swap lines with five major central banks. But Congressional hearings featured questioning of the swap lines after the 2008 crisis and their use again during the European sovereign strains of 2011–2012 generated controversy. Consequently, despite the swaps among the major central banks having become permanent, their role in the next crisis was ambiguous. On one reading, market participants anticipated swaps: non-US banks from the five swap jurisdictions could bargain for cheaper funding from money market funds in calm times. 47  Still, questions remained regarding the effective availability of swaps. In the event, when the Fed reactivated the swap lines in March 2020, there was no political reaction. Perhaps in the next crisis, the anticipation of the swap lines may calm market participants. Indeed, some observers worry that non-US banks may overdo dollar intermediation on this anticipation. Looking forward, two challenges confront the international lender of last resort as the Fed is currently playing the role. The first follows from the shift of global dollar credit from bank lending to bond markets. The second is the political dimension. 
 Bond Market Buyer of  Last Resort ? While the Fed was set up as a lender of last resort to banks, it has had to innovate to play a parallel role in securities markets. It has used its emergency powers to become a lender of last resort to securities firms, including ones not affiliated with major banks. Using the same emergency powers, in 2008 and again in 2020, the Fed bought  outstanding commercial paper  and underwrote new issues, assuring issuers, including nonfinancial corporations, of their access to credit. In 2020, the Fed used its emergency powers to buy US corporate  bonds . We have argued in Chapter  13  that the Fed’s promise to purchase US corporate  bonds  ramified widely, lifting prices of dollar bonds issued by non-US firms and sovereigns. In this case, the extension of the domestic lender of last resort to the bond market proved to serve as the international lender of last resort at one remove, or by proxy. But what if this did not work, and, as funds dumped dollar bonds issued by non-US borrowers, the market threatened to spiral downward? Such a collapse could not only inflict illiquidity and wealth losses on holders but also lead to unnecessary defaults as issuers found themselves unable to roll over maturing bonds. The US credit markets would not be immune to such developments in the global dollar bond market. One could imagine new uses for central  bank  swaps under these circumstances. For instance, the Fed could extend dollar credit to major central banks that in turn could directly buy or underwrite dollar bonds. Such an approach would follow the principle of the central bank swaps: the Fed extends dollar credit to central banks and the latter take on the credit risk of operations with the private sector. The Fed directly buying up dollar bonds of non-US issuers would depart from this principle but could benefit from speed and relative simplicity. An intermediate approach might be to have major central banks agree to indemnify the Fed for losses on bonds of ‘their’ issuers. 48 This discussion may strike the reader as far-fetched. The point is that as the US financial markets have evolved from banking to bond markets, the Fed has come to intervene in domestic securities markets as lender, buyer, and underwriter of last resort. The evolution of US financial markets has its counterpart in the dollar market outside the United States: nonbanks there have more debt in the form of bonds than bank loans these days. 49  So the question may arise of how the Fed’s intervention in the bond market might work in the international context. The practical issue of whose paper to buy is the new version of the old question of the lender of last resort: who can borrow? This brings us to the political dimension. 
 The Political Dimension Domestic lender of last resort operations can have a crucial political dimension. Events during 2008 crisis and the 2020 crisis highlight this dimension. Ball  contends that a big reason for letting Lehman fail in 2008 was the political decision by the Republican Treasury Secretary (who legally had no veto over a Fed decision) not to be seen as ‘Mr Bailout.’ 50  Ball rejects the darker interpretation that the Treasury Secretary as the former head of Goldman Sachs was happy to see off an aggressive competitor of his alma mater. 51 In 2020, the US Republican Administration supported the extension of the US domestic lender of last resort to ensure that it not be seen, as in 2008, as overly or even exclusively concerned with the fate of big banks.  The CARES Act  passed in late March 2020 put US Treasury loss-absorbing funding behind emergency Fed lending to small and medium-sized businesses and smaller non-profits under the Main  Street Lending  program. Fed purchases of municipal paper as well as bonds of the New York City transit system and the State  of Illinois  had similar backing. ‘Although Fed officials may have been reluctant to wade too far into private credit markets, they also sought to dispel notions that their emergency support was reserved for Wall Street.’ 52  A broader domestic lender of last resort operation set risky precedents but provided political cover in Congress. The international lender of last resort as practiced by the Fed drew two lines that have an inevitable political dimension. 53  In the inside circle are the major central banks that were eventually offered dollar credit to distribute to their banks with no ex ante limits. In the next circle are central banks to which the Fed offered dollar credit up to a certain amount  at times of acute funding strains . This circle comes and goes with crises, but remained the same in 2008 and 2020. In the outer circle is any central bank that holds US Treasury securities at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which can be borrowed against. The drawing of lines leaves countries out. On 28–29 October 2008, the Fed’s Open Market Committee discussed a denial of a swap line to Iceland and approaches  by Chile , India   and South Africa . 54  Other applicants were evidently  Indonesia, Peru , and  the Dominican Republic . 55 Those inclined to lay emphasis on the political basis of the choice face the question of why  the Swiss National Bank  but not  the Monetary Authority of Singapore  is among the five permanent swap partners. For the politically minded, a glance at US State Department fact sheets shows extensive US military cooperation with Singapore, while security cooperation with Switzerland seems limited to antiterrorism. 56 Looking forward, could for instance the response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 bear on the choice of dollar swap partners?  While Brazil  voted in the United Nations to condemn the invasion, it declined, like Mexico, to join the United States, its allies, and others in putting sanctions on Russia. The more general point is that the dollar is widely used by banks from countries like China where the central bank has not had a swap line with the Fed. Such banks have dollar liabilities amounting to trillions of dollars, the overwhelming majority of which are booked outside the United States. 57  Even the Fed’s provision of US banknotes could involve political considerations, as with shipment of US cash to Buenos Aires during  the Falklands/Malvinas war  in 1982. 58  So far, the crucial political dimension has not kept the international lender of last resort in dollars from working. Can central banks continue to reconcile the politically possible and the economically stabilizing in a fracturing world? Notes 1.
