           Epilogue: A Property Mania with Chinese Characteristics In September 2021, the headlines of the financial press carried warnings that China’s second largest property  developer, Evergrande , could default on a dollar bond sold offshore. Its bonds traded hands at 20 cents on the dollar, suggesting little hope that default would be avoided. After months of drama, Evergrande along with competitor Kaisa defaulted on dollar bonds in December 2021. Evergrande  had grown like topsy. It was reported to have 778 projects in 233 cities. In common with other developers, it financed itself by preselling apartments. It pre-sold 1.4 million apartments, generally for full value. The $200 billion (interest-free) obligation bulks large in its total liabilities, said to be $300 billion, including debt to banks, bondholders, and nonbanks. The firm also owes suppliers and construction firms. Along the  way, Evergrande  had diversified into electronic vehicles, health, and drones. Its chief economist had predicted in 2015 a doubling of house prices in a decade and signed on for the equivalent of $2.3 million per year in 2017. The firm pledged $115 million to  a Harvard University -led consortium to  research COVID -19 in early 2020. 1 Financial distress among developers led to a deterioration in cash flows across the big Chinese property companies. New home sales and starts have fallen by 30–40% year over year from the latter months of 2021 into 2022. By mid-2022, about a score of Chinese property companies had gone into default on most of the $100 billion of dollar bonds. The global financial press featured the question of whether China’s property market was approaching  its Minsky moment , that is, the moment of transition from mania to panic and crash. This phrase,  the Minsky moment , dates back to the Asian Financial Crisis, and was coined  by Paul McCulley , an economist at the  money manager Pacific Income Management Company  (PIMCO). 2  The term received a lot of play after the Lehman collapse in September 2008. Extraordinarily, in  2017, Zhou Xiaochuan , Governor of the People’s Bank of China, used the term to warn of over-optimism that had led to very high corporate debt and rapidly rising household debt in China. 3  (One looks hard in the memoirs of US Federal Reserve leaders and US Treasury secretaries for similar evidence of a familiarity with Minsky.) A question that divides informed observers is whether China’s leaders’ awareness of the risks of financial stability, along with the multitude of policy measures at their command, could allow them to avoid  a Minsky moment . The challenge that confronts the Chinese authorities is formidable, pressing, and threefold. First, China must adjust to the depletion of the pool of labor in the countryside that allowed millions to move to factories and cities every year. The urban share of the Chinese population rose from about 20% in 1980 to 65% in 2021. Recall that in the 1960s Germany drew in over  100,000 Turks  and Southern Europeans per year as guest workers in order to postpone, or at least to stretch out,  its ‘Lewis turning point ’ when the  excess supply of labor ran out. 4  At this turning point, an economic model based on an elastic supply of labor at the going wage requires wrenching change to slower growth. Second, China must adjust to the decline in housing investment as a source of demand. Given an already elevated share of GDP devoted to investment, an increase in the wage and consumption shares of GDP is required. And finally, and most controversially, China must adjust to lower house prices. Lower apartment prices can sap consumption by making households feel less wealthy and could threaten the solvency of some banks that have provided mortgages. Displacement: Urbanization and Privatization To start the exposition with the first stage of Minsky, the displacement that led to the Chinese property boom was the combination of rural–urban migration, a political decision, and a new means for the accumulation of household wealth. From the 1980s, hundreds of millions of Chinese would leave the countryside for the city. Never before in human history had so many left the countryside for the city. The government made a key decision to leave the giant job of housing mostly to the private sector. In the late 1990s, the government decided to sell off the stock of worker housing at state-owned enterprises at low prices to the occupants and mostly to leave the construction of new apartments to private real estate firms. By  then, Hong Kong  property companies operating on the Mainland had been building high-end, often expatriate housing, but home-grown developers came to dominate the market. From early on, it became clear that shifting from holding bank deposits paying interest rates at best modestly above the rate of inflation to buying an apartment could do wonders for one’s wealth. Seeing one’s friends becoming richer in this manner could change one’s mind about taking the risk of borrowing to the hilt, as became necessary as housing boomed. 
 Euphoria: Rising Prices and Debt, Buy-to-Wed and Buy-to-Hold In the years between displacement and distress, the Chinese property market sent out many signs of euphoria. Apartment prices multiplied. Of course, so did incomes, but the ratio of median apartment price to median income reached world-beating levels by 2018  in Beijing   and Shanghai ,  with Shenzhen  in fourth place just after  neighbor Hong Kong . In these cities, it took 40–50 years of median income to pay the price of the median apartment. 5  It took ‘only’ 20+ years in London and around 15 in Tokyo and New York. Rental yields tell a similar story. These are 1–2% in the top Chinese cities, but 3% in London and 4% in New York. Property borrowing by households rose rapidly. The state-owned banks made floating-rate mortgages a major line of business from the late 1990s. Mortgage debt has grown rapidly, pacing a more than tripling of the ratio of household credit to GDP between 2008 and end-2019. That said, household debt in China at 62% of GDP at the end of 2021 had not reached the burdens carried by households in the United States at 78% of GDP  or Hong Kong  and Great Britain, at around 90% of GDP. 6   Still, Haibin Zhu  and colleagues describe the increase in household debt as ‘alarming,’ since it brings it to the burden  of Japan  in 1989 and suggests the absence of a ‘cushion against a housing bust and potential spillover to the macroeconomy.’ 7 A Chinese characteristic of the property market has boosted mortgage debt. Chinese property developers presell apartments when they start construction. And Chinese banks extend mortgages to households at the point of purchase, before the collateral for the mortgage exists. Thus households have taken on debt through bank mortgages of purchased but uncompleted apartments. Preselling occurs in the United States in, say, Miami when its property market is hot, but it is very common in China. Property developers in China came to rely on pre-sales as their most important source of funding and faced perverse incentives. The rapid growth of projects and slow construction boosted developers’ cash flows: ‘starting construction in order to receive approval to presell projects’ while ‘stretching delivery deadlines beyond contracted deadlines.’ 8  Pressed by the authorities to reduce debt in 2021, the most leveraged property developers slowed construction. In the summer of 2022, Chinese households began to chat online about not paying on mortgages on uncompleted apartments where construction had slowed to a crawl or stopped. It is not clear whether the Chinese data on private business debt includes all of the real estate developers’ debt from pre-sold apartments. This debt is in effect construction loans by households to developers. (In recent years, developers also borrowed from households through the means of so-called wealth management products, in effect high-coupon  medium-term commercial paper  marketed by banks and near-banks.) In any case, real estate debt in the household and the business sector contributed materially to the rise in the debt of the non-government sector in China. Such debt in China has reached and surpassed the peak readings during the Japanese stock and real estate bubble of the late 1980s (Fig.  E1 ). What is more, such debt in China is well above the ratio reached by US private debt before the Great Financial Crisis of 2007–2008. If the debt owed directly by property developers to households is not well accounted for in the Chinese data, the Chinese private debt ratio may be higher than that shown by 2.5 or 5% of GDP. 9 A line graph depicts in percent of G D P versus years, with the curves of the united states, japan, china, and Germany, where japan has the maximum value. Fig. E1 Credit to the private nonfinancial sector ( Source  Refinitiv Datastream; Bank for International Settlements) In addition to high prices and high debt, the sheer contribution of property to the growth of the Chinese economy is very high. In the US housing bubble of the 2000s, the share of GDP devoted to home construction rose sharply but never exceeded a single-digit share of GDP. In China, the property market accounts for an estimated 15–20% of GDP. 10 Another important Chinese characteristic distinguished the Chinese property mania. Given the disproportion of marriageable men and women, families competed for scarce women with an apartment for the newlyweds. The more that other families offered, the more one’s own family had to offer: the essence of a rat-race. 11  Real estate acquired a social meaning absent from other asset classes. But the number of marriages in China has been declining since 2013. A related but distinct salient characteristic is the demand for empty apartments as a portfolio asset. Bank deposit and bond yields have tended to be low in relation to nominal GDP growth, albeit generally positive in real terms. Capital controls have generally bound, despite leaks. And wealth management products offering juicy returns are relatively recent innovations and fraught with credit risk. In most markets, a speculative demand for housing shows up as ‘buy to let.’ But in China, the social value attached to newness in apartments (and cars) is high. Moreover, as prices have risen relative to incomes, they have also risen in relation to rents, so the reward for renting at 1–2% in the top Chinese cities is low. So rather than buying to let, Chinese investors ‘buy to hold’ empty. This produces not so much the infamous ghost cities, but rather a Swiss cheese of empty apartments in generally occupied buildings. An estimated 22% of Chinese households own more than one home. 12 The fraction of the urban housing stock that is owned but vacant is naturally a matter of some dispute. An analysis  at Capital Economics , an economic consultancy, agrees with Chinese analysts on a vacancy rate of about 20% but highlights that half of the empty apartments are old privatized stock awaiting sale to a developer and demolition. 13  On this reckoning there could be 30–50 million owned but empty recently constructed apartments in China’s cities, storing value more than housing people. A consequence of high prices, high rates of home ownership, and the portfolio demand for housing is that housing wealth represents a very high fraction of household wealth. One estimate puts housing wealth at 60% of urban households’ portfolios. 14 
 From Distress to Panic and Crash? Clearly, Chinese residential real estate has entered distress. Developers’ business models depended on growth to generate cash and did not take into account the prospective decline in rural-urban migration. Developers are defaulting or scrambling not to. Housing activity is declining rapidly, although prices are declining only marginally in the official data. Government policies are shifting gears from restraining to promoting housing investment. Residential investment as a share of GDP is bound to fall in China. US residential investment fell by almost two-thirds between the end of 2005 and the end of 2010. Even with stepped-up government investment in housing, residential investment could fall by 10% of GDP in China. Normally real estate prices grind down overextended periods, but the Chinese characteristic of a large portfolio demand for housing could speed things up. As developers slash prices to move inventory, they undermine the store of value motive. Those who bought to hold most recently among the holders of the 30–50 million empty apartments, might put their apartments on the market. And as prices declined further, less recently acquired empty apartments could be offered for sale, and so on. A substantial fall in housing prices in China would tend to lower consumption, given the high share of housing wealth in household assets. This would only increase the challenge of adapting to the change in labor supply and only make it more difficult to adjust to the decline of residential investment spending as a share of output. A sustained decline in Chinese property would ramify globally. Chinese residential blocks stand tall thanks to steel milled from tons and tons of Australian iron ore and metallurgical coal. The wealth represented by residential property sends millions of Chinese tourists and students abroad. Lower Chinese demand for commodities and lower Chinese interest rates to offset economic weakness would put downward pressure on the renminbi and other emerging market and commodity currencies. Another Chinese characteristic, heavy government involvement in the housing sector, is often cited as a reason not to anticipate a crash. The consolidated government sector depends on land sales for 25% of its revenue, with local governments particularly dependent on them. 15  And local governments have borrowed substantially, in effect using land sales as a fall-back means to service debt should project revenues prove disappointing. Government finances are vulnerable to a property downturn, but this gives the Chinese authorities even more reason to manage the real estate market. Not least, the Chinese government at various levels has  used macroprudential policy  to manage the property market. Controls on borrowing and other measures have been turned on and they can be turned off. Indeed, the strains in the finances of the Chinese property developers in the fall of 2021 were in part owing to the ‘three red lines’ drawn by the Chinese authorities that set limits on their leverage. Now, to support the property market, the government can provide guarantees on the bonds of selected developers and guide banks to lend to them. In addition, as noted, the authorities have the scope to reduce interest rates in general and the mortgage rate benchmark in particular. Those who argue that the government can prevent a property crash emphasize its capacity to use administrative means to prevent a major home price decline. 16  They also cite the need for public housing to enable those who have lived in the cities without proper household registration to settle down. They also cite China’s capital controls that limit the diversification of household assets. It is an open question how the authorities will manage the challenges of the decline in housing demand and the decline in house prices in China. The stakes are high. Notes 1.
